pulls: Ecclesiastes does not begin by fixing your life. It begins by telling you the truth about it — so that Christ can be the answer instead of the next thing you try.
paras: Ecclesiastes opens the way an honest life actually opens — not with a promise, but with a sigh. “Vanity of vanities.” The word is hevel: vapor, breath, a mist you reach for and close your hand on nothing. Before the Preacher teaches you a single thing, he tells you the truth about the air you have been breathing your whole life. Everything under the sun, chased for its own sake, comes up empty in the end.

And the arresting part is this: the man saying this is the last man on earth who should be able to. This is not the complaint of someone who never got his chance. Solomon had wealth, wisdom, power, peace, and every pleasure a human being can name. He had it all and tried it all, and when he laid it on the scale and weighed it, it registered as vapor. If the richest, wisest man who ever lived came up empty, the problem was never that he lacked enough. The problem is the sun he was living under — a life measured only by what happens between the horizons, with God left out.

That is the dust this study is written from. Not the dust of failure only, but the dust of a soul that has everything and still aches. The psalmist prays, “My soul clings to the dust; Revive me according to Your word” (Psalm 119:25, NKJV). Ecclesiastes is twelve chapters of a man clinging to the dust, saying it out loud, refusing to pretend. Your job this week is not to argue him out of it. It is to sit in it honestly — and then to lift up your eyes.

parts.label: PART ONE
parts.heading: THE VERDICT: VAPOR
paras: The Preacher states his thesis before he defends it: “Vanity of vanities, all is vanity.” He is not being dramatic. He is being a doctor who refuses to lie to a dying patient. Hevel is not “life is bad.” It is “life, held onto by itself, will not hold you.” Grab it and it slips. Bank on it and it breaks. The vapor is not a mood; it is a measurement, taken by the one man who had the most to weigh.

Notice what he asks in verse 3: “What does man gain from all his labor in which he labors under the sun?” That phrase — under the sun — is the key that unlocks the whole book. It means life reckoned on the horizontal only, God factored out, nothing counted but what happens between sunrise and sunset. Read under that sun, everything really is vapor. The Preacher is not lying about the world. He is telling you exactly what the world is worth when you try to make it your everything.

parts.label: PART TWO
parts.heading: THE TREADMILL OF THE WORLD
paras: Then he holds up a mirror made of creation itself. Generations come and go; the earth stays and swallows them (v. 4). The sun goes down and hurries back to the place where it rises (v. 5). The wind turns south, then north, then back, going everywhere and arriving nowhere (v. 6). The rivers run into the sea, and the sea is not full (v. 7). Round and round it goes, effort without arrival, motion without meaning.

You know this treadmill. It is the ache underneath the productive week — the sense that you are running hard and the finish line keeps moving. “The eye is not satisfied with seeing, nor the ear filled with hearing” (v. 8). You get the thing you wanted and the wanting simply relocates. This is not a flaw in your discipline. It is the built-in restlessness of a soul that was made for God trying to live on everything but God.

parts.label: PART THREE
parts.heading: NOTHING NEW, NO ONE REMEMBERED
paras: The Preacher lands two more blows, and they are the honest ones you spend most of your energy avoiding. First: “There is no new thing under the sun” (v. 9). The novelty you are chasing is a repackaging of something already tried, already tired. Second, and heavier: “There is no memory of the former; neither shall there be any memory of the latter” (v. 11). The legacy you are building will be forgotten. The name you are making will be a blank someone walks past.

You spend enormous energy outrunning verse 11. You build so you will be remembered. The Preacher, with nothing left to prove, tells you the finish line of that race: you will be forgotten, and so will your children. It sounds cruel until you see what it is doing. He is knocking every idol out of your hands — not to leave you empty-handed, but to turn your hands upward.

parts.label: PART FOUR
parts.heading: WHY THE DUST NEEDS THIS
paras: A believer should welcome this bracing chapter instead of flinching from it. Solomon’s dead end is a mercy. Every road he closes is a road that would have cost you your life to keep walking. When he says the world cannot satisfy you, he is not stealing your joy; he is telling you where joy is not, so you will stop bleeding out looking for it there.

There is a name that never appears in Solomon’s survey of life “under the sun,” and that absence is the whole point. Everything under the sun is vapor. But you were not made to live under the sun. You were made for the One who made the sun, and the ache proves it. This world cannot satisfy you; only Christ can — the One “who gave himself for our sins, that he might deliver us out of this present evil age” (Galatians 1:4). So come to Ecclesiastes dusty, and let it empty your hands, because empty hands are the only ones that can take hold of Him.

stations.verse: ‘Vanity of vanities,’ says the Preacher; ‘Vanity of vanities, all is vanity.’ What does man gain from all his labor in which he labors under the sun?
stations.question: Where in your life are you laboring hardest “under the sun” for a gain that keeps slipping through your fingers?
stations.live: Name one “vapor” you keep gripping as if it were solid. Open your hand around it in prayer today, and ask God to be the weight your soul actually rests on.
body: Hevel is the Preacher’s signature word — he uses it nearly forty times. Its root sense is vapor or breath: your breath on a cold morning, there for a second and gone. The same Hebrew spelling is the name Abel (Genesis 4:2), the son whose life was cut short. Solomon is not saying the world is evil; he is saying it is ungraspable. You cannot build a life on breath. Anything under the sun, clutched as your everything, will mist away in your hand exactly when you need it to hold.

stations.verse: All things are full of weariness beyond uttering. The eye is not satisfied with seeing, nor the ear filled with hearing.
stations.question: What is the restlessness you feel after getting what you wanted trying to tell you about what you were made for?
stations.live: The next time you feel bone-tired from wanting, say it plainly to God: “This is weariness. I bring it to You.” Then rest in something you did not earn.
body: Yagea is the adjective the Preacher reaches for when he says all things are “full of weariness.” Moses uses the same word for Israel on the road out of Egypt — faint and weary, with the stragglers picked off behind them (Deuteronomy 25:18). It is the tiredness of a long march, not a short nap. Solomon says the whole created round wears that way: the eye never full, the ear never done. The weariness is not proof that you are weak. It is proof that the march was never meant to end at the horizon.

stations.verse: There is no memory of the former; neither shall there be any memory of the latter that are to come, among those that shall come after.
stations.question: How much of your labor is really an attempt to be remembered?
stations.live: Write down one thing you are building mainly so you will be remembered. Hand it to God by name, and ask Him to be the One who remembers you.
body: Zikron is a memorial — the marker that keeps a thing in mind after it is gone. The Preacher says flatly that the former things have none, and the latter things will have none either. He says it again of the wise man in 2:16: no memory forever. Every monument you raise under the sun is written in chalk. That is exactly why the gospel matters: your name is kept by the God who does not forget His own, not by the men who come after you.

stations.verse: ‘Don’t lay up treasures for yourselves on the earth, where moth and rust consume, and where thieves break through and steal; but lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven, where neither moth nor rust consume, and where thieves don’t break through and steal; for where your treasure is, there your heart will be also.
stations.question: Where is your treasure stored right now — under the sun, or with Christ?

stations.verse: Then I looked at all the works that my hands had worked, and at the labor that I had labored to do; and behold, all was vanity and a chasing after wind, and there was no profit under the sun.
stations.question: If you made Solomon’s honest review of what you are building, what would you have to admit?
stations.gloss: advantage, profit, what is left over
stations.live: Look at the week ahead and ask of each big task, “What am I hoping is left over from this?” Let the answer drive you to Christ, not harder into the task.
body: Yitron is a ledger word: the profit, the surplus, what remains after the costs are paid. The Preacher asks the question in 1:3 and answers it in 2:11 — “there was no profit under the sun.” Asked again in 3:9, it gets the same silence. Under the sun, the books never balance in your favor. The only lasting surplus is one you did not earn: the righteousness of Christ credited to a man with nothing left on his side of the ledger.

stations.verse: who gave himself for our sins, that he might deliver us out of this present evil age, according to the will of our God and Father—
stations.question: Where are you still asking this present evil age to give you what only your Deliverer can?

stations.verse: Therefore let’s also, seeing we are surrounded by so great a cloud of witnesses, lay aside every weight and the sin which so easily entangles us, and let’s run with perseverance the race that is set before us, looking to Jesus, the author and perfecter of faith, who for the joy that was set before him endured the cross, despising its shame, and has sat down at the right hand of the throne of God.
stations.question: What would it look like this week to run “looking to Jesus” rather than running to be seen?
stations.gloss: to look away from all else, to fix one’s gaze upon
stations.live: Choose one moment each day this week — before the phone, before the news — to look away from everything else and fix your eyes on Christ in one verse.
body: Aphoraō is built on the verb “to see” with a prefix meaning “away from.” It is not a glance. It is looking away from everything else to fix on one thing. Ecclesiastes shows you a treadmill with no finish; Hebrews shows you a race with a Person at the end of it. The runner does not win by watching the other lanes. He wins by keeping his eyes on Jesus, who has already run it, endured the cross, and sat down.
pulls: You will not out-labor the vapor. But the same soul that clings to the dust can lift its eyes to the One the dust was never able to hold.

practices.title: NAME YOUR “UNDER THE SUN”
practices.body: Every man has a horizon he secretly lives beneath — the arena where he is quietly trying to make life add up: career, reputation, the next achievement, the approval of a certain few. This week, catch yours. When your mood rises and falls with it, say out loud: “This is under the sun. It was never able to hold me.” Naming the vapor is the first step to stop banking on it.

practices.title: LET THE ACHE PREACH
practices.body: The next time you get the thing you wanted and feel the wanting simply move on, do not scold yourself and do not chase the next thing. Stop and let the restlessness testify: “I was made for more than this can give.” Augustine said it in the first lines of his Confessions: the heart is restless until it rests in God. Treat the ache as a signpost, not a defect.

practices.title: BRING YOUR LEDGER TO THE SON
practices.body: Solomon reviewed his whole portfolio and called it wind. Do the same on purpose — but bring the review to Jesus. Take the thing you are most proud of building and the thing you are most afraid of losing, and pray: “Neither of these is my life. You are.” Let Christ, not your record, be where your soul rests.

practices.title: ASK THE SPIRIT FOR FIXED EYES
practices.body: Ecclesiastes is a book about eyes that are never satisfied. The remedy is eyes that are fixed. You cannot manufacture that focus; the Spirit gives it. Each morning this week, before your feet hit the floor, pray one honest sentence: “Holy Spirit, the world keeps pulling my eyes down. Fix them on Christ today.” Then watch for the moments your gaze actually lifts.

practices.title: SAY THE DUST OUT LOUD
practices.body: The dust thrives in isolation. Before the week ends, tell one trusted brother the honest thing Ecclesiastes surfaced in you — the place life is feeling like vapor — and ask him to remind you where real hope is. Grace spoken out loud is grace that starts to stick.

title: The Dust Under the Sun
subtitle: when everything gained still comes up empty
keyVerse: ‘Vanity of vanities,’ says the Preacher; ‘Vanity of vanities, all is vanity.’

passage.text: The words of the Preacher, the son of David, king in Jerusalem:
“Vanity of vanities,” says the Preacher; “Vanity of vanities, all is vanity.”
What does man gain from all his labor in which he labors under the sun?
One generation goes, and another generation comes; but the earth remains forever.
The sun also rises, and the sun goes down, and hurries to its place where it rises.
The wind goes toward the south, and turns around to the north. It turns around continually as it goes, and the wind returns again to its courses.
All the rivers run into the sea, yet the sea is not full. To the place where the rivers flow, there they flow again.
All things are full of weariness beyond uttering. The eye is not satisfied with seeing, nor the ear filled with hearing.
That which has been is that which shall be; and that which has been done is that which shall be done: and there is no new thing under the sun.
Is there a thing of which it may be said, “Behold, this is new?” It has been long ago, in the ages which were before us.
There is no memory of the former; neither shall there be any memory of the latter that are to come, among those that shall come after.

stationsLabel: THE WORD ON LIFE UNDER THE SUN
stationsIntro: Read each passage slowly, with your Bible open if you can. Do not rush to the question. Let the verse land first, then answer honestly in the lines provided — and where a Hebrew or Greek word is opened up, let it sharpen the verse you just read.
lifeTitle: Where the Vapor Meets Real Life
lifeIntro: This week is not about pretending life under the sun is better than the Preacher says. It is about letting his honesty do its work — emptying your hands of what cannot hold you, so they are free to take hold of Christ.
prayer: Father, I have been chasing life under the sun. I have gripped vapor and called it solid. I come back to You with empty hands. Lord Jesus, You are what the world could never be. You gave Yourself to deliver me from this present evil age. I take hold of You. Holy Spirit, fix my restless eyes on Christ today. Revive me according to Your word. Amen.
prayerLines: Father, I have been chasing life under the sun.
I have gripped vapor and called it solid.
I come back to You with empty hands.
Lord Jesus, You are what the world could never be.
You gave Yourself to deliver me from this present evil age.
I take hold of You.
Holy Spirit, fix my restless eyes on Christ today.
Revive me according to Your word. Amen.
bottomLine: Life under the sun is vapor, and it was never meant to be your everything. Solomon proves it so Christ can be your only hope instead of your last resort. Let this week empty your hands so they are free to take hold of Him.
benediction: Before this study asks you to change a thing, it wants you to look up and admit what the Preacher already knows: the ground is dust, and the air is vapor. Everything under the sun — the labor, the wisdom, the pleasure, the name you are making — runs its circle and comes up empty. That is not cynicism. It is the truth, spoken by the one man who had the most to lose by telling it. And he tells it as a mercy, so you will stop bleeding out on roads that were never going anywhere.

So lift up your eyes. When your work feels like a treadmill with no finish, lift up your eyes — there is a race with a Person at the end of it. When you fear you will be forgotten, lift up your eyes — your name is held by the One who bought you, and He does not forget. When the thing you gained still leaves you aching, lift up your eyes — the ache was a signpost home all along.

This is dust to revival, and it begins exactly here: a soul clinging to the ground, honest at last, and Christ, who gave Himself to deliver you out of this present evil age, standing over the dust with His hand out. You were not made for what is under the sun. You were made for Him.
closingVerse: You were dust chasing vapor under the sun. In Christ you are a soul with somewhere to rest.
carry: Where are you still living as though something under the sun could finally satisfy you?

pulls: Wisdom can name the vapor with perfect clarity. It cannot make the vapor hold you. Only the One who gives wisdom can do that.
paras: If the world cannot satisfy the soul, surely understanding the world can. That is the next thing the dust reaches for — not pleasure this time, but insight. If you could just figure it out, get wise enough, read enough, master the pattern, then you could stand above the vapor and finally feel solid ground. It is the most respectable of all the substitutes, because it looks like the opposite of foolishness. And Solomon, of all people, was qualified to test it.

“I have obtained for myself great wisdom above all who were before me in Jerusalem” (1:16). This is not a man dabbling. This is the wisest man who ever lived, applying the sharpest mind in history to the deepest questions of existence — and reporting back. His report is not what the dust wants to hear: “this also was a chasing after wind” (1:17). The chase after understanding is the chase after wind with a diploma on the wall.

And then he says the thing almost no one will admit out loud: knowing more did not lessen the ache — it sharpened it. “For in much wisdom is much grief; and he who increases knowledge increases sorrow” (1:18). The more clearly he saw, the more clearly he saw what was wrong. Understanding is real, and it is good, and it cannot save you. It can diagnose the disease with perfect precision and hand you no cure.

parts.label: PART ONE
parts.heading: THE EXPERT TAKES THE STAND
paras: Solomon opens by establishing his credentials, and he is not bragging — he is telling you not to dismiss what comes next. “I, the Preacher, was king over Israel in Jerusalem” (1:12). He is not a bitter man who never got his shot. He had the throne, the resources, the mind, and the freedom to chase understanding as far as a human being can chase it. When such a man says the search came up empty, you cannot wave it off as sour grapes.

He says, “I applied my heart to seek and to search out by wisdom concerning all that is done under the sky” (1:13). Notice the horizon again — under the sky, under the sun. He is trying to make sense of everything on the horizontal, and he calls the project what it is: “a heavy burden that God has given to the sons of men to be afflicted with.” The relentless human drive to figure it all out is real, God-given even — and on its own terms it grinds you down.

parts.label: PART TWO
parts.heading: WHAT WISDOM CANNOT FIX
paras: Then comes one of the most quietly devastating lines in the book: “That which is crooked can’t be made straight; and that which is lacking can’t be counted” (1:15). There are twists in this world that no amount of insight will untwist. Why do the wicked prosper? Why do the innocent suffer? Why does the story break where it breaks? The wisest man alive looked straight at the crooked places and admitted his wisdom could not straighten them.

This is where worldly brilliance always dead-ends. The more of it a man acquires, the more sharply he sees the unanswered questions — and the fewer tools he has to answer them. Understanding, cut off from the Creator, becomes a flashlight that only shows you more of the dark. There is a floor beneath the crooked places, but it is not made of information. It is made of trust in a sovereign God who holds what you cannot straighten.

parts.label: PART THREE
parts.heading: ONE FATE FOR THE WISE AND THE FOOL
paras: In chapter 2 Solomon presses the knife in further. Yes, “wisdom excels folly, as far as light excels darkness” (2:13) — he is not a cynic who thinks learning is worthless. The wise man sees where he is going; the fool walks in the dark. And yet “one event happens to them all” (2:14). The wise man and the fool arrive at the same grave: “the wise man must die just like the fool!” (2:16).

That is the wall wisdom cannot climb. It can make your seventy years clearer, wiser, better-steered — and then it lays you in the identical ground as the man who wasted his. If death takes the wise and the foolish alike, then wisdom, for all its light, cannot be the thing that saves you. Solomon’s conclusion is brutal and honest: “So I hated life ... for all is vanity and a chasing after wind” (2:17). He had climbed to the top of the ladder of understanding and found it leaning against nothing.

parts.label: PART FOUR
parts.heading: WHERE TRUE WISDOM BEGINS
paras: So is the pursuit of wisdom a dead end? Only the kind that stays under the sun. Solomon is emptying a specific hand — the hand that grips knowledge as its savior — so that it can take hold of a different kind of wisdom altogether. “The fear of Yahweh is the beginning of wisdom” (Proverbs 9:10). Real wisdom does not start with mastering the world; it starts with bending the knee to the One who made it.

And the New Testament names where that wisdom finally lives: “Christ Jesus, who was made to us wisdom from God” (1 Corinthians 1:30). The answers Solomon could not find by climbing were given in a Person you can only receive. The cross looks like foolishness to the wise of this age — and it is the very wisdom of God, the place where the crooked was made straight and the grave that swallows the wise and the fool alike was itself undone. You will not think your way home. But you can be carried there by the One who is wisdom in the flesh.

stations.verse: I applied my heart to seek and to search out by wisdom concerning all that is done under the sky. It is a heavy burden that God has given to the sons of men to be afflicted with.
stations.question: Where are you trying to “figure out” your way to peace, as if enough understanding would finally make you secure?
stations.live: Name the problem you keep turning over at night. Say it to God before you sleep, and leave the task with Him until morning.
body: Inyan is the Preacher’s word for the job in front of you — the task, the business, the thing that fills the day. In 1:13 the search itself is the inyan: “a heavy burden that God has given to the sons of men to be afflicted with.” In 2:23 it is the travail that keeps a man’s heart from rest even at night. The search for answers is a real task God has laid on men. It was never meant to be carried as a way of saving yourself. Christ carries the weight you cannot.

stations.verse: For in much wisdom is much grief; and he who increases knowledge increases sorrow.
stations.question: Where has knowing more only made the ache sharper for you?
stations.live: When a hard truth stings this week, do not argue with the sting. Take it straight to Christ and ask Him to use it to make your heart good.
body: Ka‘as is grief with an edge — vexation, the ache that has anger in it. The Preacher says much wisdom brings much of it. Clear sight does not heal the wound; it just lets you see its full size. In 7:3 he uses the same word for the sorrow by which “the heart is made good.” Grief can drive you deeper into yourself, or it can drive you to God. Knowledge alone cannot choose which. Only grace turns vexation into a good heart.

stations.verse: The wise man’s eyes are in his head, and the fool walks in darkness—and yet I perceived that one event happens to them all. Then I said in my heart, ‘As it happens to the fool, so will it happen even to me; and why was I then more wise?’ Then I said in my heart that this also is vanity. For of the wise man, even as of the fool, there is no memory forever, since in the days to come all will have been long forgotten. Indeed, the wise man must die just like the fool!
stations.question: Where have you been trusting your own good sense to save you instead of your Savior?
stations.live: Ask one person you trust to name a place where you will not be taught. Listen without defending yourself.
body: Kesil is the fool of Proverbs and Ecclesiastes — not a man without a brain, but a man who will not be taught. He walks in darkness and thinks he sees. The sting of 2:14–16 is that the wise man and the kesil end up in the same grave. The line between them is real in life and erased at death. Only one thing can cross that line from the other side: the resurrection of Jesus, who walked out of the grave that levels everyone.

stations.verse: The fear of Yahweh is the beginning of wisdom. The knowledge of the Holy One is understanding.
stations.question: Where do you need the fear of Yahweh to become the starting point of your thinking again?
stations.live: Before you read, study, or research anything this week, pray one line: “Holy One, let me know You first.” Then begin.
body: Da‘at is knowing — perception, discernment, the grasp of how things are. In Ecclesiastes 1:18 more of it brings more sorrow. In Proverbs 9:10 the same word takes a different object: “the knowledge of the Holy One is understanding.” That is the whole difference. Knowledge of the world, held under the sun, ends in grief. Knowledge of the Holy One, given by grace, is life. And in 2:26 the Preacher says it plainly: God gives knowledge to the man who pleases Him.

stations.verse: Where is the wise? Where is the scribe? Where is the lawyer of this world? Hasn’t God made foolish the wisdom of this world? For seeing that in the wisdom of God, the world through its wisdom didn’t know God, it was God’s good pleasure through the foolishness of the preaching to save those who believe. For Jews ask for signs, Greeks seek after wisdom, but we preach Christ crucified: a stumbling block to Jews, and foolishness to Greeks, but to those who are called, both Jews and Greeks, Christ is the power of God and the wisdom of God; because the foolishness of God is wiser than men, and the weakness of God is stronger than men.
stations.question: Where is your pride still embarrassed by a wisdom you cannot achieve, only receive?
stations.gloss: to make foolish, to show to be foolish
stations.live: Name one argument you rely on to feel safe with God. Set it down this week and rest on the cross instead.
body: Mōrainō means to make foolish or to show up as foolish. Paul asks, “Hasn’t God made foolish the wisdom of this world?” The cross did what Solomon could only describe: it exposed the whole ladder of worldly understanding as leaning on nothing. In Romans 1:22 the same verb describes men who claimed to be wise and “became fools.” God is not against your mind. He is against your mind as a savior, and He made that savior foolish at Calvary.

stations.verse: Because of him, you are in Christ Jesus, who was made to us wisdom from God, and righteousness and sanctification, and redemption:
stations.question: What would change if you stopped trying to be wise enough and rested in the One who is your wisdom?

stations.verse: But if any of you lacks wisdom, let him ask of God, who gives to all liberally and without reproach, and it will be given to him.
stations.question: What would it look like this week to simply ask God for the wisdom you have been striving to acquire?
pulls: The wisest man who ever lived climbed to the top of understanding and found it leaning on nothing. Then God gave wisdom in a Person, and told you to ask.

practices.title: CATCH THE “IF I JUST UNDERSTOOD” REFLEX
practices.body: Anxiety loves to disguise itself as research. When you are afraid, you analyze — replaying, searching, strategizing — as though enough understanding would finally make you safe. This week, catch it. When you notice yourself spiraling into figuring-it-out, stop and say: “I do not need to understand this to be held by God. He does.” Let trust interrupt the analysis.

practices.title: LET THE CROOKED PLACES DRIVE YOU TO GOD
practices.body: There are things in your life that will not be straightened by insight — a loss, a diagnosis, a question with no clean answer. Solomon admitted it: what is crooked can’t be made straight. Instead of grinding yourself down trying to solve the unsolvable, bring it to the God who holds what you cannot fix, and pray: “I cannot make this straight. I trust the One who can.”

practices.title: BRING YOUR CLEVERNESS TO THE SON
practices.body: You will be tempted this week to lean on being the smart one — to trust your read of the situation more than you trust Christ. Reverse it. Take the area where you feel most competent and lay it down: “Jesus, You are my wisdom. I stop trusting my own understanding to save me here.” Competence is a gift; it is a terrible savior.

practices.title: ASK THE SPIRIT FOR THE FEAR OF GOD
practices.body: The beginning of wisdom is not information; it is reverence — and the Spirit is the One who gives it. Each morning this week, before you reach for answers, pray one honest sentence: “Holy Spirit, teach me to fear God rightly, so my knowing does not curdle into sorrow.” Then watch how differently the day’s problems look from a posture of awe.

practices.title: ASK, INSTEAD OF ONLY SEARCHING
practices.body: James says the wisdom Solomon spent a lifetime hunting is available for the asking. Before the week ends, name one decision where you have been striving to be wise enough, and simply ask: “Father, I lack wisdom here. You promised to give it liberally. I am asking.” Then tell one brother you are learning to ask rather than only strive.

title: Wisdom Cannot Save the Dust
subtitle: when knowing more only makes the ache sharper
keyVerse: For in much wisdom is much grief; and he who increases knowledge increases sorrow.

passage.text: I, the Preacher, was king over Israel in Jerusalem.
I applied my heart to seek and to search out by wisdom concerning all that is done under the sky. It is a heavy burden that God has given to the sons of men to be afflicted with.
I have seen all the works that are done under the sun; and behold, all is vanity and a chasing after wind.
That which is crooked can’t be made straight; and that which is lacking can’t be counted.
I said to myself, “Behold, I have obtained for myself great wisdom above all who were before me in Jerusalem. Yes, my heart has had great experience of wisdom and knowledge.”
I applied my heart to know wisdom, and to know madness and folly. I perceived that this also was a chasing after wind.
For in much wisdom is much grief; and he who increases knowledge increases sorrow.

stationsLabel: THE WORD ON WISDOM UNDER THE SUN
stationsIntro: Read each passage slowly, with your Bible open if you can. Do not rush to the question. Let the verse land first, then answer honestly in the lines provided — and where a Hebrew or Greek word is opened up, let it sharpen the verse you just read.
lifeTitle: Where the Limits of Wisdom Meet Real Life
lifeIntro: This week is not about despising knowledge — wisdom is a gift, and Solomon says as much. It is about moving your trust off your own understanding and onto the God who gives wisdom and became it in Christ.
prayer: Father, I cannot think my way to peace. I have leaned on my own understanding and called it strength. I come to You with the crooked places I cannot straighten. Lord Jesus, You were made to me wisdom from God. You went into the grave that takes the wise and the fool alike, and You came out. I rest in You. Holy Spirit, teach me the fear of God today. Let my knowing bend the knee. Amen.
prayerLines: Father, I cannot think my way to peace.
I have leaned on my own understanding and called it strength.
I come to You with the crooked places I cannot straighten.
Lord Jesus, You were made to me wisdom from God.
You went into the grave that takes the wise and the fool alike, and You came out.
I rest in You.
Holy Spirit, teach me the fear of God today.
Let my knowing bend the knee. Amen.
bottomLine: Wisdom is a gift and a good, but it was never meant to be your savior. It can name the vapor with perfect clarity and still leave you in the grave beside the fool. Move your trust off your own understanding and onto Christ, who was made to you wisdom from God.
benediction: Before this week asks you to be wiser, it wants you to admit where wisdom ran out. The sharpest mind in history applied itself to the deepest questions of life and came back with a verdict that stings: this also was a chasing after wind, and in much wisdom is much grief. You have felt it — the way understanding a hard thing more clearly only makes it hurt more precisely. Solomon is not mocking knowledge. He is telling you its ceiling, so you will stop asking it to be your roof.

So lift up your eyes. When the crooked places of your life refuse to straighten, lift up your eyes — there is a God who holds what you cannot fix. When your best thinking leaves you at the same grave as the fool, lift up your eyes — there is One who walked out of that grave. When you are tired of being smart enough, lift up your eyes — Christ was made to you wisdom from God, and He is not a technique to master but a Person to receive.

This is dust to revival, and it turns here: a soul that has stopped trusting its own understanding, on its knees before the Holy One. You were never meant to think your way home. The One who is wisdom in the flesh came down into the dust to carry you there.
closingVerse: You cannot think your way out of the dust. But the God who is wisdom itself came down into it.
carry: Where are you still trusting your own understanding to save you?

pulls: Solomon denied himself nothing and came up empty. Pleasure makes a good gift and a bottomless god — and the dust keeps confusing the two.
paras: Are you content? Or is there always something — just one or two things — that, if they were different, would finally make you happy? A little more money, a different job, a change in your circumstances, and then the ache would quiet. Almost every man lives leaning slightly forward toward that next thing. And Solomon, the one man in history with the power to actually reach every next thing at once, runs the experiment so you do not have to run it with your life.

“Come now, I will test you with mirth: therefore enjoy pleasure” (2:1). He does not test it halfway. He builds houses, plants vineyards, lays out gardens and parks and pools; he gathers silver and gold and singers and every delight a man can name. “Whatever my eyes desired, I didn’t keep from them. I didn’t withhold my heart from any joy” (2:10). Read that slowly. He denied himself nothing. If satisfaction could be bought, poured, or indulged into a soul, Solomon’s soul would have been full to the brim.

And the verdict is one short, honest sentence: “behold, all was vanity and a chasing after wind, and there was no profit under the sun” (2:11). The man who withheld nothing came up with nothing. That is not a warning against joy — Ecclesiastes will later call food and work and love gifts from God’s hand. It is a warning against asking pleasure to be your god. Pleasure is a good servant and a devouring master, and the dust keeps trying to worship what was only ever meant to be enjoyed.

parts.label: PART ONE
parts.heading: THE GREAT EXPERIMENT
paras: Solomon runs the test no one else could afford. “I made myself great works. I built myself houses. I planted myself vineyards. I made myself gardens and parks ... I also gathered silver and gold for myself” (2:4–8). Reread that list and notice the drumbeat: myself, myself, myself. This is a soul curved entirely inward, spending unlimited resources on a single project — its own happiness.

And he keeps his wisdom through the whole thing: “My wisdom also remained with me” (2:9). This is not a drunk fumbling in the dark; it is a clear-eyed man sampling every pleasure deliberately, taking notes. Which is exactly what makes his conclusion so heavy. He is not saying, “I overdid it and got sick of it.” He is saying, “I did it thoroughly, wisely, completely — and it still would not fill me.”

parts.label: PART TWO
parts.heading: THE LIE UNDERNEATH IT ALL
paras: There is an old lie humming beneath every pleasure-chase, and it is older than Solomon. From the garden onward, the serpent has whispered that satisfaction can be found apart from God — that you can have the fruit without the Giver. “Eat, drink, and be merry” is the house philosophy of the rich fool in Luke 12, and your culture has it stitched into everything it sells.

Be honest about how deep it runs. If the gospel were quietly removed from your life, would your weekly pursuit of comfort and pleasure change at all? That is how thoroughly the lie gets swallowed. Solomon’s experiment is written down in Scripture to keep you from spending your one life proving what he already proved — that the fruit, apart from the Giver, always rots in your hand.

parts.label: PART THREE
parts.heading: “I HAVE THIS COMING”
paras: Watch how Solomon accounts for the whole indulgence: “my heart rejoiced because of all my labor, and this was my portion from all my labor” (2:10). Portion. His share. What he had coming. There it is — the sentence the dust says to itself right before it reaches for something it will regret. I worked hard. I have earned this. Just this once. The logic feels airtight, and it has led more men into ruin than open rebellion ever did.

Maybe for you it is spending you cannot afford, charged just this once. Maybe it is a pleasure your flesh is calling a reward. Maybe it is numbing out because the week was heavy and surely you deserve to escape. The “I have this coming” gate is where so much dust gets in. Solomon walked through that gate with a wisdom and a treasury you will never match — and on the far side of it he found the same empty air.

parts.label: PART FOUR
parts.heading: WHERE THE ACHE WAS POINTING
paras: So must a believer become grim, joyless, suspicious of every good thing? Never. The verdict is not “pleasure is evil.” The verdict is “pleasure cannot be God.” And the ache you feel when the pleasure fades is not your enemy — it is a signpost. Every good thing that leaves you still hungry is quietly pointing past itself to the only One who satisfies.

Jesus stood and cried out, “If anyone is thirsty, let him come to me and drink!” (John 7:37). He is not against your joy; He is the source of it — “In your presence is fullness of joy. In your right hand there are pleasures forever more” (Psalm 16:11). The dust does not need to stop enjoying. It needs to stop worshiping the gift and lift its eyes to the Giver — and there, at last, the enjoying becomes full instead of frantic.

stations.verse: I said in my heart, ‘Come now, I will test you with mirth: therefore enjoy pleasure;’ and behold, this also was vanity. I said of laughter, ‘It is foolishness;’ and of mirth, ‘What does it accomplish?’
stations.question: Where are you quietly running Solomon’s experiment right now, hoping the next pleasure will finally quiet the ache?
stations.live: Notice one place this week where you reach for a laugh to avoid a hard thought. Face the thought with God first, and then laugh freely.
body: Sechoq is laughter — the sound of the party. Solomon says of it, “It is foolishness,” and in 7:3 he goes further: “Sorrow is better than laughter.” That is not because laughter is wrong. It is because laughter chased as an escape is thin; it drowns out the question instead of answering it. Psalm 126:2 uses the same word for a different laughter: “our mouth was filled with laughter” when God brought His people home. That laughter comes after rescue, not instead of it.

stations.verse: Whatever my eyes desired, I didn’t keep from them. I didn’t withhold my heart from any joy, for my heart rejoiced because of all my labor, and this was my portion from all my labor.
stations.question: What are you really telling yourself when you say “I’ve earned this” right before you reach for something you later regret?
stations.live: Take one good thing you enjoy this week and say out loud, “This is my portion from God’s hand, not my wages.” Then enjoy it without clutching.
body: Cheleq is a portion — the share of land or goods allotted to you. Solomon calls his pleasures “my portion from all my labor.” Later he uses the same word more gently: to rejoice in your work is your portion (3:22); life with the wife you love is your portion (9:9). A portion is a gift you receive, not a debt the world owes you. The danger is treating the portion as the whole inheritance. Your real inheritance is God Himself, given to you in Christ.

stations.verse: Then I looked at all the works that my hands had worked, and at the labor that I had labored to do; and behold, all was vanity and a chasing after wind, and there was no profit under the sun.
stations.question: If you made Solomon’s honest audit of what you chase for pleasure, what would you have to admit?
stations.live: Name the one pursuit you would be most afraid to call “chasing wind.” Pray about it by name before you pour another hour into it.
body: Re‘ut is the word behind “a chasing after wind.” It carries the sense of striving or longing — running after something you want. Put it with “wind” and you have the whole book in a picture: a man running full speed after air. The Preacher uses the phrase again and again, as if to make sure you hear it every time you start the chase. The wind cannot be caught. But the Spirit, who is the true breath of God, is given freely to those who believe.

stations.verse: I will tell my soul, ‘Soul, you have many goods laid up for many years. Take your ease, eat, drink, and be merry.’ ’ ‘But God said to him, ‘You foolish one, tonight your soul is required of you. The things which you have prepared—whose will they be?’ So is he who lays up treasure for himself, and is not rich toward God.’
stations.question: Where are you laying up pleasure for yourself instead of becoming rich toward God?
stations.gloss: to be rich, to become rich
stations.live: This week give away one thing you have been storing up for your own comfort — money, time, or a possession — and thank Christ for the riches He gave you.
body: Plouteō means to be rich. Jesus ends the story of the fool with a turn: the man was rich in barns and poor “toward God.” Solomon had the barns too, and found them empty. Paul uses the same verb in 2 Corinthians 8:9 to describe the gospel itself: though Christ was rich, He became poor, so that you through His poverty might become rich. You cannot become rich toward God by storing up. You become rich by receiving what Christ emptied Himself to give.

stations.verse: As the deer pants for the water brooks, so my soul pants after you, God. My soul thirsts for God, for the living God. When shall I come and appear before God?
stations.question: What do you usually reach for first when your soul feels dry?
stations.live: When your soul feels dry this week, say to it out loud, “You thirst for the living God.” Then open the Word before you open anything else.
body: Tsame is plain thirst — a dry throat and a body that needs water. “My soul thirsts for God, for the living God.” The psalmist does not pretend the thirst away, and he does not pour anything else down it. He names what it is for. Solomon tried to quench the same thirst with every pleasure the world had. Isaiah 49:10 promises a people who will not thirst, led by the One who has mercy on them. Jesus stood up and claimed to be that water.

stations.verse: Now on the last and greatest day of the feast, Jesus stood and cried out, ‘If anyone is thirsty, let him come to me and drink! He who believes in me, as the Scripture has said, from within him will flow rivers of living water.’
stations.question: Where are you still going to the world’s wells for a thirst only Christ can quench?

stations.verse: You will show me the path of life. In your presence is fullness of joy. In your right hand there are pleasures forever more.
stations.question: What would it look like this week to seek your joy in God’s presence instead of under the sun?

stations.verse: Not that I speak because of lack, for I have learned in whatever state I am, to be content in it. I know how to be humbled, and I also know how to abound. In everything and in all things I have learned the secret both to be filled and to be hungry, both to abound and to be in need.
stations.question: What are you still waiting to have changed before you will let yourself be content?
pulls: The world hands you broken cisterns and calls them fountains. Christ stands up and says, Come to Me and drink.

practices.title: CATCH THE “I HAVE THIS COMING”
practices.body: The most dangerous sentence in your week is not “I want this” — it is “I’ve earned this.” That is the gate Solomon walked through. This week, when you feel the reward-reflex rising before a purchase, a pleasure, an escape, stop and name it: “That is the ‘I deserve it’ voice.” Naming it breaks its spell long enough to ask what you are really hungry for.

practices.title: RECEIVE THE GIFT WITHOUT WORSHIPING IT
practices.body: You do not have to renounce pleasure to be free of it — you have to reorder it. This week, take one real pleasure (a meal, a rest, a good moment) and consciously receive it from God: “Thank You for this gift. I enjoy it in Your hand, and I do not ask it to be You.” Gratitude turns a would-be idol back into a gift.

practices.title: BRING YOUR CRAVINGS TO THE SON
practices.body: When the deep appetite cries out this week — for comfort, for escape, for the next thing — do not just resist it and do not just feed it. Bring it to Jesus: “Lord, this thirst is real, and only You can satisfy it. You said to come to You and drink, so here I am.” Let the craving drive you to Christ instead of the cistern.

practices.title: ASK THE SPIRIT FOR CONTENTMENT
practices.body: Contentment is not a personality trait; Paul says he learned it, and the Spirit is the teacher. Each morning this week, pray one honest sentence: “Holy Spirit, teach me the secret of being content in Christ today, whether I get the thing I want or not.” Then watch for the moments the grasping loosens and you can simply rest.

practices.title: SPEAK TO YOUR SOUL OUT LOUD
practices.body: The psalmist did not just feel his cravings; he talked back to them. When your soul reaches for a pleasure to fill the ache, answer it out loud: “Soul, you thirst for God, not for this.” And before the week ends, tell one trusted brother the pleasure you are most tempted to make your god, so grace spoken aloud can loosen its grip.

title: Pleasure Cannot Fill the Dust
subtitle: when you deny yourself nothing and still come up empty
keyVerse: Whatever my eyes desired, I didn’t keep from them. I didn’t withhold my heart from any joy, for my heart rejoiced because of all my labor, and this was my portion from all my labor. Then I looked at all the works that my hands had worked, and at the labor that I had labored to do; and behold, all was vanity and a chasing after wind, and there was no profit under the sun.

passage.text: I said in my heart, “Come now, I will test you with mirth: therefore enjoy pleasure;” and behold, this also was vanity.
I said of laughter, “It is foolishness;” and of mirth, “What does it accomplish?”

I searched in my heart how to cheer my flesh with wine, my heart yet guiding me with wisdom, and how to lay hold of folly, until I might see what it was good for the sons of men that they should do under heaven all the days of their lives.
I made myself great works. I built myself houses. I planted myself vineyards.
I made myself gardens and parks, and I planted trees in them of all kinds of fruit.
I made myself pools of water, to water from it the forest where trees were grown.
I bought male servants and female servants, and had servants born in my house. I also had great possessions of herds and flocks, above all who were before me in Jerusalem.

I also gathered silver and gold for myself, and the treasure of kings and of the provinces. I got myself male and female singers, and the delights of the sons of men: musical instruments, and that of all sorts.
So I was great, and increased more than all who were before me in Jerusalem. My wisdom also remained with me.
Whatever my eyes desired, I didn’t keep from them. I didn’t withhold my heart from any joy, for my heart rejoiced because of all my labor, and this was my portion from all my labor.
Then I looked at all the works that my hands had worked, and at the labor that I had labored to do; and behold, all was vanity and a chasing after wind, and there was no profit under the sun.

stationsLabel: THE WORD ON PLEASURE UNDER THE SUN
stationsIntro: Read each passage slowly, with your Bible open if you can. Do not rush to the question. Let the verse land first, then answer honestly in the lines provided — and where a Hebrew or Greek word is opened up, let it sharpen the verse you just read.
lifeTitle: Where the Emptiness of Pleasure Meets Real Life
lifeIntro: This week is not a call to joylessness — God gives pleasure as a gift, and Ecclesiastes will say so plainly. It is a call to stop asking pleasure to be your god, and to receive it instead from the hand of the One who satisfies.
prayer: Father, I have been chasing pleasure to fill what only You can fill. I have told myself I had it coming. I come back to You thirsty. Lord Jesus, You stood and called the thirsty to come and drink. I come to You. Holy Spirit, teach me contentment in Christ today. Let me receive every good thing from His hand and never again ask a gift to be my God. Amen.
prayerLines: Father, I have been chasing pleasure to fill what only You can fill.
I have told myself I had it coming.
I come back to You thirsty.
Lord Jesus, You stood and called the thirsty to come and drink.
I come to You.
Holy Spirit, teach me contentment in Christ today.
Let me receive every good thing from His hand
and never again ask a gift to be my God. Amen.
bottomLine: The man who denied himself nothing came up with nothing, and he wrote it down so you would not have to spend your life proving it again. Pleasure is a gift, not a god. Move your worship off the gift and onto the Giver, and bring your thirst to Christ.
benediction: Before this week asks you to give anything up, it wants you to face what Solomon already proved: the man who withheld nothing from himself came up empty-handed. Houses, gardens, gold, music, every pleasure his eyes could name — and at the end of it, a chasing after wind. That is not because pleasure is wicked. It is because pleasure was never built to be a god, and a soul made for God cannot be filled by anything less, no matter how much of it you pour in.

So lift up your eyes. When the old reward-reflex whispers that you have earned the next thing, lift up your eyes — Christ is a better portion than anything under the sun. When a good pleasure fades and leaves you still hungry, lift up your eyes — the hunger was a signpost pointing home all along. When you are tired of drinking from cisterns that never hold water, lift up your eyes — Jesus is still standing, still calling the thirsty to come to Him and drink.

This is dust to revival, and it turns here: a soul that has stopped worshiping the gift and has come to the Giver. In His presence is fullness of joy. In His right hand are pleasures forever more. Enjoy every good thing as a gift from that hand, and drink where the thirst was always meant to be filled.
closingVerse: You denied yourself nothing and stayed thirsty. Christ is the fountain — come and drink.
carry: Where are you still asking pleasure to be your god?

pulls: Work is not the enemy of the soul — work cut off from God is. Take Him out, and even a masterpiece comes out to vapor.
paras: There is one substitute for God more respectable than pleasure and more socially rewarded than wisdom: work. Not lazy escape but honest labor — building something, providing, achieving, leaving a mark. If a soul cannot be satisfied by what it enjoys or what it understands, surely it can be satisfied by what it accomplishes. So Solomon turns the searchlight onto the one arena every culture applauds, and reports back with words that land like a stone: “I hated all my labor” (2:18).

Read that again, because it is shocking coming from him. This is the most productive man who ever lived — houses, vineyards, gardens, a kingdom — saying he came to hate the fruit of his own labor. And his reason is one you cannot argue with: “I must leave it to the man who comes after me. Who knows whether he will be a wise man or a fool?” (2:18–19). Everything you build, you build for someone whose name you may not even know, who may squander in a season what cost you your life to gather.

Solomon’s arithmetic is brutal. Labor is not the problem. Success is not the problem. The problem is labor cut off from the God it was meant to serve — work aimed only at what happens under the sun, with no eternal weight and no eternal hand to receive it. Take God out of it, and even a flawless career comes out to vapor. Leave Him in, and the same eating and drinking and working become, in Solomon’s own words, “from the hand of God” (2:24).

parts.label: PART ONE
parts.heading: THE GRIEF OF THE HANDOFF
paras: Solomon’s despair in this passage is not the complaint of a man who failed — it is the ache of a man who succeeded completely and then did the math. “Therefore I began to cause my heart to despair concerning all the labor in which I had labored under the sun” (2:20). Someday, sooner than he wanted, he would lay down his tools for the last time and lose all say over everything he had made. In the grave you do not manage your estate. You do not steer your legacy. You hand it off, and the handoff is a gamble.

You have felt the edge of this even if you have never named it. The project you poured yourself into gets reorganized the year after you leave. The savings you sacrificed for get spent in ways you would grieve. The reputation you guarded fades within a generation. Solomon is not being morbid; he is being honest about a truth you spend enormous energy not looking at: you cannot take it with you, and you cannot control what happens to it once you are gone.

parts.label: PART TWO
parts.heading: THE SUM THAT NEVER COMES OUT
paras: Watch what Solomon actually indicts. He does not say work is bad, or that skill is worthless, or that providing for your family is vanity. He says labor “under the sun” — labor cut off from God — comes up empty no matter how it turns out. “For what does a man have of all his labor and of the striving of his heart, in which he labors under the sun? For all his days are sorrows, and his travail is grief; yes, even in the night his heart takes no rest” (2:22–23).

There it is: even in the night his heart takes no rest. That is the tell of a life built on the wrong foundation — the lying awake, the churning, the load you cannot set down because your identity is welded to your output. When work becomes the thing that justifies you, it can never give you rest, because the ledger is never finished and the verdict is never in. Labor without God is not just empty at the end; it is exhausting the whole way through.

parts.label: PART THREE
parts.heading: LIGHT BREAKING THROUGH
paras: And then, for the first time in the book, a real ray of light breaks the gloom: “There is nothing better for a man than that he should eat and drink, and make his soul enjoy good in his labor. This also I saw, that it is from the hand of God” (2:24). Notice the hinge — from the hand of God. The very same eating, drinking, and working that were vapor when chased for their own sake become gift the moment they are received from God’s hand.

To the man who pleases Him, “God gives wisdom, knowledge, and joy” (2:26). The satisfaction Solomon hunted everywhere was never hiding inside the work itself. It was always in the Giver, waiting to be received rather than seized. The change is not that you work less or achieve less. The change is whose hand you take it from.

parts.label: PART FOUR
parts.heading: WORKING AS FOR THE LORD
paras: The New Testament takes this ray and turns it into daylight. Paul tells ordinary workers: “whatever you do, work heartily, as for the Lord, and not for men, knowing that from the Lord you will receive the reward of the inheritance; for you serve the Lord Christ” (Colossians 3:23–24). There is the inheritance Solomon feared losing — not left to an unknown heir, but received from the Lord Himself and kept where no fool can squander it.

This is how the dust’s labor is redeemed. The same hands that labored in despair under the sun can labor in worship for the Lord. Your work does not have to justify you — Christ has already done that — so it is finally free to become an offering instead of a verdict. And because “your labor is not in vain in the Lord” (1 Corinthians 15:58), even the smallest faithful task done for Him carries a weight the grave cannot erase. You will still leave your work behind. You will not leave behind the One you did it for.

stations.verse: I hated all my labor in which I labored under the sun, because I must leave it to the man who comes after me. Who knows whether he will be a wise man or a fool? Yet he will have rule over all of my labor in which I have labored, and in which I have shown myself wise under the sun. This also is vanity.
stations.question: What are you building right now that you will one day have to hand off with no control over what happens to it?
stations.live: Name the labor that is wearing you down right now. Before you begin it this week, hand it up: “This is Yours, and I do it for You.”
body: Amal is not neutral work — it is labor that wears you down, effort with sweat and trouble in it. Solomon pounds this word through chapter 2 to describe the striving that fills his days and steals his sleep. But the same book that calls amal vapor also says a man can “make his soul enjoy good in his labor” when he receives it from God’s hand (2:24). The labor does not change; the source does. Amal chased for itself grinds you to dust. Amal offered to God becomes a place where joy can grow.

stations.verse: For what does a man have of all his labor and of the striving of his heart, in which he labors under the sun? For all his days are sorrows, and his travail is grief; yes, even in the night his heart takes no rest. This also is vanity.
stations.question: Where does your work follow you into the night and refuse to let you rest?
stations.live: Tonight, before sleep, name aloud the striving still running in your heart. Tell God you are laying it down, and leave it there until morning.
body: Ra‘yon is a close cousin of the “chasing after wind” phrase. In 2:22 it is “the striving of his heart” — the inner reaching that goes on even after the hands stop. That is why the heart takes no rest at night. The body quits; the ra‘yon keeps running. Solomon knew it from the inside. Only a man whose standing is settled by someone else can finally let the heart lie down. In Christ, your standing is settled.

stations.verse: There is nothing better for a man than that he should eat and drink, and make his soul enjoy good in his labor. This also I saw, that it is from the hand of God. For who can eat, or who can have enjoyment, more than I?
stations.question: Where are you still trying to squeeze satisfaction out of your labor instead of receiving it from God’s hand?

stations.verse: Also that every man should eat and drink, and enjoy good in all his labor, is the gift of God.
stations.question: What good thing in your work have you been treating as a wage you earned rather than a gift you were given?
stations.live: Pick one good thing in your work this week — a skill, an outcome, a moment of satisfaction — and say, “Thank You; this was a gift, not a wage.”
body: Mattat is a gift — something handed to you by another, not wages drawn from your own account. The Preacher uses it twice for the same surprising thing: the power to eat, drink, and enjoy good in your labor “is the gift of God” (3:13; 5:19). This is the great reversal of the whole book. What the dust exhausts itself trying to achieve, God gives. The open hand that receives a gift holds more than the clenched fist that grabs a wage.

stations.verse: And whatever you do, work heartily, as for the Lord, and not for men, knowing that from the Lord you will receive the reward of the inheritance; for you serve the Lord Christ.
stations.question: How would working “as for the Lord” change the way you show up to your labor this week?
stations.gloss: recompense, reward, a giving back in return
stations.live: Choose one thankless task this week and do it carefully, telling Christ, “This one is for You.”
body: Antapodosis is a repayment — a giving back in return. In the New Testament it appears only here: “from the Lord you will receive the reward of the inheritance.” Solomon dreaded leaving his inheritance to a stranger. Paul says the true inheritance comes from the Lord, and He gives it back in full. The reward is not wages you earned by your work; it is an inheritance, which means it comes to sons. You serve the Lord Christ, and He does not forget what was done for Him.

stations.verse: Therefore, my beloved brothers, be steadfast, immovable, always abounding in the Lord’s work, because you know that your labor is not in vain in the Lord.
stations.question: Which work in your life would you do differently if you truly believed it would not be wasted?
stations.live: Pick one faithful duty you have been tempted to quit because it seems pointless. Keep at it this week, and each time, remember the empty tomb.
body: Ametakinētos means immovable — not shifted from your place. It too appears only here in the New Testament. Paul says it right after the resurrection chapter: because death has been swallowed up in victory, you can stand firm and keep working, knowing your labor is not in vain in the Lord. Solomon’s labor was shifted and scattered by death. Yours is anchored by an empty tomb.
pulls: You will hand off everything you build. But labor offered to the Lord is not left to a fool. It is received by Him, and it is not in vain.

practices.title: NAME WHAT YOU ARE ADDING UP
practices.body: Solomon’s sum was work plus success minus God, and it always came out to vapor. This week, catch the moments you are running that sum — striving as though the outcome decides your worth. When you feel the churn rise, say out loud: “My labor does not justify me. Christ already did.”

practices.title: HAND THE WORK UP BEFORE YOU START
practices.body: Before you begin a task this week — a shift, a job, a hard conversation — pause for one sentence: “Father, this is Yours. I do it for You, not to prove myself.” Offering the work before you do it changes the whole thing. The same labor becomes worship instead of a courtroom.

practices.title: RECEIVE THE GOOD AS A GIFT, NOT A WAGE
practices.body: When something in your work goes well this week, resist the reflex to bank it as proof of your value. Receive it from the Son: “Thank You, Jesus — this was a gift from Your hand, not a wage I earned.” Gratitude loosens the grip that turns good work into an idol.

practices.title: ASK THE SPIRIT FOR REST YOU CANNOT MANUFACTURE
practices.body: If your work follows you into the night, you cannot out-discipline your way to rest — but the Spirit gives it. Each evening this week, pray one honest sentence: “Holy Spirit, I lay this labor down before You. Give me the rest my striving cannot.” Then let the unfinished list stay unfinished in God’s hands overnight.

practices.title: INVEST A LITTLE WHERE IT CANNOT BE LOST
practices.body: Everything you build under the sun will be handed off. So this week, deliberately pour some labor into what lasts — a word of encouragement, an act of quiet service, time given to someone who cannot repay you. Tell one trusted brother what you did, and ask him to help you keep aiming your work higher than the horizon.

title: The Work of Your Hands
subtitle: when everything you build must be left to someone else
keyVerse: There is nothing better for a man than that he should eat and drink, and make his soul enjoy good in his labor. This also I saw, that it is from the hand of God.

passage.text: I turned myself to consider wisdom, madness, and folly; for what can the king’s successor do? Just that which has been done long ago.
Then I saw that wisdom excels folly, as far as light excels darkness.
The wise man’s eyes are in his head, and the fool walks in darkness—and yet I perceived that one event happens to them all.
Then I said in my heart, “As it happens to the fool, so will it happen even to me; and why was I then more wise?” Then I said in my heart that this also is vanity.
For of the wise man, even as of the fool, there is no memory forever, since in the days to come all will have been long forgotten. Indeed, the wise man must die just like the fool!
So I hated life, because the work that is worked under the sun was grievous to me; for all is vanity and a chasing after wind.
I hated all my labor in which I labored under the sun, because I must leave it to the man who comes after me.
Who knows whether he will be a wise man or a fool? Yet he will have rule over all of my labor in which I have labored, and in which I have shown myself wise under the sun. This also is vanity.
Therefore I began to cause my heart to despair concerning all the labor in which I had labored under the sun.
For there is a man whose labor is with wisdom, with knowledge, and with skillfulness; yet he shall leave it for his portion to a man who has not labored for it. This also is vanity and a great evil.
For what does a man have of all his labor and of the striving of his heart, in which he labors under the sun?
For all his days are sorrows, and his travail is grief; yes, even in the night his heart takes no rest. This also is vanity.
There is nothing better for a man than that he should eat and drink, and make his soul enjoy good in his labor. This also I saw, that it is from the hand of God.
For who can eat, or who can have enjoyment, more than I?

For to the man who pleases him, God gives wisdom, knowledge, and joy; but to the sinner he gives travail, to gather and to heap up, that he may give to him who pleases God. This also is vanity and a chasing after wind.

lifeTitle: Where the Futility of Work Meets Real Life
lifeIntro: This week is not a call to stop working or to care less — Scripture honors honest labor. It is a call to take God out of the margins of your work and put Him back at the center, so your labor becomes an offering instead of a verdict.
prayer: Father, my work has been carrying a weight only You can carry. I have asked it to justify me, and it cannot. I bring it back to You. Lord Jesus, You finished the work I could never finish. I work for You today, not for a verdict You already gave. Holy Spirit, give me rest I cannot manufacture. Let my labor be an offering, and let me receive its good as a gift from Your hand. Amen.

I have asked it to justify me, and it cannot.
I bring it back to You.
Lord Jesus, You finished the work I could never finish.
