and let me receive its good as a gift from Your hand. Amen.
bottomLine: The most productive man who ever lived came to hate his own labor, because everything built under the sun must be handed off. But the same work becomes gift the moment it is received from God’s hand and offered back to Him. Stop asking your labor to justify you, and work as for the Lord.
benediction: Before this week asks you to work harder, it wants you to hear the confession of a man who worked as hard as anyone ever has and came to hate the fruit of it. Solomon built a kingdom and still lay awake at night, because everything he made he would have to leave to someone else, and no amount of success could quiet the ache underneath. That is the dead end of labor under the sun. Not that work is worthless — that work alone was never able to carry the weight of a soul.

So lift up your eyes. When your work follows you into the night and will not let you rest, lift up your eyes — Christ calls the weary to Himself. When you grieve that everything you build will be handed off, lift up your eyes — the inheritance that matters comes from His hand and is kept where no fool can waste it. When you are tired of laboring to justify yourself, lift up your eyes — the verdict was already spoken at a cross, and now your work is free to be worship.

This is dust to revival, and it turns here: a soul that has stopped asking its labor to save it. Christ rose from the dead, and because He lives, your labor is not in vain in the Lord. Receive your work from His hand, and give it back to Him.
closingVerse: You cannot take your work with you. Offered to the Lord, it is not in vain.
carry: Where have you been asking your work to justify you?

pulls: The seasons of your life are not falling loose in the dark. They are set by a hand you can trust — the same hand that put eternity in your heart.
paras: Something quietly shifts in chapter three, and if you miss it you miss the turn the whole book has been waiting to make. For two chapters Solomon has been living “under the sun” — measuring life on the flat horizontal and finding only vapor. Now he speaks of “a time for every purpose under heaven” (3:1). Same world, wider lens. And from that higher vantage, the churning of chapter one turns out not to be random at all.

“For everything there is a season.” Then comes the famous litany — a time to be born and a time to die, to plant and to pluck up, to weep and to laugh, to mourn and to dance, to keep silence and to speak. Fourteen pairs, the whole range of a human life. These are not accidents you stumble into. They are appointed times, and — this is the part the dust resists — you are not the one who sets them. Another hand holds the calendar.

That truth is either a terror or a comfort, depending on whose hand you believe is holding the pen. To a soul living under the sun, “you don’t control your seasons” is a nightmare. But to a soul that has lifted its eyes, it is the beginning of rest. The times of your life are not tumbling loose in the dark. They are being set, one by one, by a God who “has made everything beautiful in its time” and who “has also set eternity in their hearts” (3:11) — an ache for forever planted in creatures bound by time, so that you would look up from the seasons to the One who made them.

parts.label: PART ONE
parts.heading: UNDER HEAVEN, NOT JUST UNDER THE SUN
paras: Back in chapter one, Solomon watched the sun rise and set, the wind turn, the rivers run, and he called it all vanity — pointless repetition, a chasing after wind. Now in chapter three he looks at the very same rhythms of life and calls them times God has made fitting. What changed was not the world. What changed was the altitude of his gaze.

This is the difference the whole book turns on. Under the sun, life is a treadmill of meaningless motion. Under heaven, the same motions are the ordered work of God. The believer does not get a different set of seasons than everyone else — birth and death, planting and plucking up, weeping and laughing come to all. What the believer gets is a different lens: the confidence that a sovereign hand is behind the calendar.

parts.label: PART TWO
parts.heading: APPOINTMENTS YOU DID NOT MAKE
paras: You think of appointments as things you schedule — you set the time, you control the calendar. Solomon strips that illusion away. There is a time for every purpose, and you are not the one setting it. That is the uncomfortable center of the passage: the seasons of your life are set by God, not by you.

The dust hates this, because the dust wants to be in charge of its own weather. You want the season of joy to stay and the season of loss never to come, and you spend enormous energy trying to schedule your life around your preferences. But there is a strange mercy in surrender here. If the appointments are yours to keep, then every hard season is a failure you must have caused. If the appointments are God’s, then even the season you would never have chosen has an Author — and an aim you cannot yet see.

parts.label: PART THREE
parts.heading: ETERNITY IN THE HEART
paras: In the middle of the passage comes one of the most piercing sentences in all of Scripture: “He has also set eternity in their hearts, yet so that man can’t find out the work that God has done from the beginning even to the end” (3:11). God has planted a sense of forever inside creatures who live in time. That is why the seasons never fully satisfy — why even the good ones leave a residue of longing. You were built with a homesickness for eternity that nothing under the sun can cure.

This is the ache Ecclesiastes has been circling from page one, finally named. No pleasure fills you, no achievement completes you, no season is quite enough, because eternity is in your heart, and time cannot hold what eternity was made for. The restlessness is not a defect. It is a compass. God set forever in you so that the not-enough of every season would keep pointing you past the seasons, up to Himself.

parts.label: PART FOUR
parts.heading: NOTHING RANDOM FOR THE MAN IN CHRIST
paras: So how does a dusty soul live in seasons it did not choose and cannot control? Not by pretending to be the author, and not by despairing that no one is. By trusting the hand that holds the calendar. For the man whose faith rests on Christ, there are no random events and no wasted appointments. Even the season you would have begged to skip is held by a God who works “all things ... together for good for those who love God” (Romans 8:28).

And the eternity in your heart has a name and a face. The homesickness points to a home; the longing points to a Person. Jesus stepped into human seasons — born in one, weeping in one, dying in one — and rose to open the door to the forever your heart was made for. So you can hold your seasons with open hands. The good ones you receive as gifts and the hard ones you endure with hope, because the hand that set the appointment is the pierced hand that will not let you go. “My times are in your hand” (Psalm 31:15).

stations.verse: For everything there is a season, and a time for every purpose under heaven: a time to be born, and a time to die; a time to plant, and a time to pluck up that which is planted;
stations.question: Which season are you actually in right now?
stations.gloss: a set time, an appointed time
stations.live: Say out loud the name of the season you are in. Then pray, “You set this time. I will meet You in it.”
body: Zeman is the word behind “For everything there is a season.” It means a set time — a time fixed in advance. In the tagged Hebrew text of Ecclesiastes it appears only here, at the head of the poem, like a heading over the whole list. Everything that follows — birth and death, weeping and dancing — falls under it. Your seasons are not improvised. They are set, and the One who sets them is not careless with your life.

stations.verse: He has made everything beautiful in its time. He has also set eternity in their hearts, yet so that man can’t find out the work that God has done from the beginning even to the end.
stations.question: Where do you feel the ache of eternity in your heart most sharply?
stations.live: When a good moment this week leaves you strangely unsatisfied, name it: “This is the eternity in my heart.” Let it lift your eyes past the season to Christ.
body: Olam is the long reach of time beyond sight — forever, the everlasting. The earth “remains forever” (1:4), and whatever God does “shall be forever” (3:14). In 3:11 God has set olam in the human heart: a creature bound by seasons, carrying inside it a craving for the eternal. That is the deepest reason nothing under the sun satisfies. The ache is not a malfunction; it is a homing signal, and Christ, who has the words of eternal life, is where it lands.

stations.verse: I know that whatever God does, it shall be forever. Nothing can be added to it, nor anything taken from it; and God has done it, that men should fear before him.
stations.question: Where do you need to rest in God’s sovereignty instead of your own control this week?
stations.gloss: to add, to increase, to do again
stations.live: Name one thing you keep adding to your walk with God as if it made you more secure. Thank Christ this week that nothing needs adding to His work.
body: Yasaf is to add or increase. In 1:18 it is the man who “increases knowledge” and so increases sorrow — adding that only subtracts. In 3:14 the same verb turns around: whatever God does, “nothing can be added to it.” Your life is full of adding — more effort, more control, more insurance. God’s work needs none of it. What He has done in Christ is finished, and you cannot add to it, only rest in it.

stations.verse: But I trust in you, Yahweh. I said, ‘You are my God.’ My times are in your hand. Deliver me from the hand of my enemies, and from those who persecute me.
stations.question: What worry about timing do you need to move out of your grip and into God’s hand this week?
stations.gloss: to snatch away, to deliver, to rescue
stations.live: Pray David’s words each morning this week: “My times are in your hand. Deliver me.” Name the thing you need Him to rescue you from.
body: Natsal is to snatch out — to pull someone from danger. David says, “My times are in your hand. Deliver me.” The two go together. Because the calendar is in God’s hand, the rescue is in God’s hand too. Jacob prayed the same verb before meeting Esau: “Please deliver me” (Genesis 32:11). You do not have to force your own rescue. The One who holds your times is the One who snatches His people out.

stations.verse: We know that all things work together for good for those who love God, for those who are called according to his purpose.
stations.question: Which hard season do you need to trust God is working together for good, even before you can see the pattern?

stations.verse: But when the fullness of the time came, God sent out his Son, born to a woman, born under the law, that he might redeem those who were under the law, that we might receive the adoption of children.
stations.question: Where can you trust God’s timing in the thing you are waiting on right now?
stations.live: Write down the thing you are waiting on. Beside it, write “the fullness of the time came.” Look at it each day this week.
body: Plērōma is fullness — the thing that fills something up. “When the fullness of the time came, God sent out his Son.” God kept His greatest appointment neither early nor late. John uses the same word for what Christ gives: “From his fullness we all received grace upon grace” (John 1:16). The time was filled up, and then the One came who fills you up. Your waiting is not wasted on a God who kept that appointment.
pulls: Your times are in His hand. The same God who sent His Son in the fullness of the time is keeping every appointment of your life.

practices.title: NAME THE SEASON YOU ARE ACTUALLY IN
practices.body: Half of your discontent is fighting the season you are in while pining for a different one. This week, name your actual season honestly — grief, waiting, planting, harvest, silence — and stop demanding it be something else. Say it plainly to God: “This is the season You have set. I will meet You in this one, not the one I wish I had.”

practices.title: RELEASE THE TIMING YOU CANNOT CONTROL
practices.body: There is something you are trying to rush or force right now — an answer, a change, a resolution. This week, deliberately put its timing back in God’s hand: “This has its time, and You hold the calendar, not me.” Loosening your grip on the timeline is one of the truest acts of trust a dusty soul can make.

practices.title: LET THE ACHE POINT YOU TO THE SON
practices.body: When a good moment leaves you unsatisfied this week, do not scramble to fill the gap. Recognize it: this is the eternity God set in your heart, refusing to be filled by anything less than Him. Bring the longing to Jesus: “You are the home this ache is pointing to.”

practices.title: ASK THE SPIRIT FOR TRUST IN THE HARD SEASON
practices.body: You cannot talk yourself into peace about a season you did not choose — but the Spirit can give it. Each morning this week, pray one honest sentence: “Holy Spirit, I cannot see the pattern yet. Help me trust that this time is in my Father’s hand.” Then watch for the small steadyings only He can give.

practices.title: SAY “MY TIMES ARE IN YOUR HAND” OUT LOUD
practices.body: When anxiety about the future rises this week — the delay, the unknown, the appointment you dread — answer it with David’s words spoken aloud: “My times are in your hand.” And tell one trusted brother the season you are learning to trust God through, so he can steady you when the waiting feels long.

title: A Season for Everything
subtitle: when the appointments of your life are set by another hand
keyVerse: For everything there is a season, and a time for every purpose under heaven:

passage.text: For everything there is a season, and a time for every purpose under heaven:
a time to be born, and a time to die; a time to plant, and a time to pluck up that which is planted;
a time to kill, and a time to heal; a time to break down, and a time to build up;
a time to weep, and a time to laugh; a time to mourn, and a time to dance;
a time to cast away stones, and a time to gather stones together; a time to embrace, and a time to refrain from embracing;
a time to seek, and a time to lose; a time to keep, and a time to cast away;
a time to tear, and a time to sew; a time to keep silence, and a time to speak;
a time to love, and a time to hate; a time for war, and a time for peace.
What profit has he who works in that in which he labors?
I have seen the burden which God has given to the sons of men to be afflicted with.
He has made everything beautiful in its time. He has also set eternity in their hearts, yet so that man can’t find out the work that God has done from the beginning even to the end.
I know that there is nothing better for them than to rejoice, and to do good as long as they live.
Also that every man should eat and drink, and enjoy good in all his labor, is the gift of God.
I know that whatever God does, it shall be forever. Nothing can be added to it, nor anything taken from it; and God has done it, that men should fear before him.
That which is has been long ago, and that which is to be has been long ago. God seeks again that which is passed away.

lifeTitle: Where the Appointed Seasons Meet Real Life
lifeIntro: This week is not about passive resignation to whatever happens — it is about active trust in the God who sets your seasons. It means holding your times with open hands instead of a white-knuckled grip.
prayer: Father, I have been fighting the season You set. I wanted to hold the calendar myself. I bring my times back to You. Lord Jesus, You came in the fullness of the time. You are the eternity my heart aches for. Holy Spirit, help me trust the hand that holds my days, even where I cannot see. My times are in Your hand. Amen.

I wanted to hold the calendar myself.
I bring my times back to You.
Lord Jesus, You came in the fullness of the time.
You are the eternity my heart aches for.

bottomLine: The seasons of your life are not tumbling loose in the dark. They are set by a God who put eternity in your heart so the ache would keep pointing you home. Move your grip off the calendar you cannot control and onto the hand that holds it.
benediction: Before this week asks you to endure your season, it wants you to see whose hand set it. For two chapters Solomon stared at the churn of life from below and called it vanity. Then he lifted his eyes and saw the very same events as times — a time for everything, set not by you but by God. The world did not change. His gaze did. And from the higher vantage, the random dark of the seasons turned out to be the ordered work of a sovereign hand.

So lift up your eyes. When you are stuck in a season you would never have chosen, lift up your eyes — it is an appointment, not an accident, held by the God who makes everything fitting in its time. When a good moment still leaves you aching, lift up your eyes — that ache is eternity in your heart, pointing to the only One who can fill it. When the timing of your life feels out of control, lift up your eyes — your times are in His hand, the same hand that sent the Son in the fullness of the time.

This is dust to revival, and it turns here: a soul that has stopped trying to author its own seasons. Christ was born in the fullness of the time, died at the hour the Father set, and rose on the third day as promised. The God who kept those appointments is keeping yours.
closingVerse: Your seasons are appointments, not accidents, and the hand that sets them is the pierced hand that will not let you go.
carry: What season are you fighting that God has set?

pulls: The world offers you power or pity, and neither one comforts. But there is a Friend who sticks closer than a brother, and a cord of three strands that will not break.
paras: Solomon has emptied your hands of pleasure, wisdom, and work. Now he lifts his eyes from his own experiment and looks out at the world — and what he sees is a hard, unsentimental picture the dust knows all too well. “Behold, the tears of those who were oppressed, and they had no comforter; and on the side of their oppressors there was power; but they had no comforter” (4:1). He says it twice: no comforter. The wound of a broken world is not only that it is unjust. It is that it is lonely.

This chapter is Ecclesiastes at its most honest about two aches every soul carries: the ache of a world that is not fair, and the ache of being alone in it. Solomon looks at oppression so relentless he concludes the dead are better off than the living, and the never-born better off than both (4:2–3). That is not despair for its own sake. It is a man refusing to paper over a world where the powerful crush the weak and no comfort seems to come. If you have ever wept and felt no one was there, Solomon is not going to pretend you did not.

But watch where he goes. Having stared at the loneliness of a fallen world, he hands you the counter-truth the whole chapter is built toward: “Two are better than one ... For if they fall, the one will lift up his fellow ... and a threefold cord is not quickly broken” (4:9–12). You were not made to face the dust alone. And the deepest comfort the friendless world cannot give, the God who came near gives — for there is “a friend who sticks closer than a brother” (Proverbs 18:24).

parts.label: PART ONE
parts.heading: THE TEARS WITH NO COMFORTER
paras: Solomon does something brave here: he refuses to look away from injustice. He does not offer a tidy explanation. He does not tell the sufferer to cheer up. He sits in the raw fact that under the sun, the powerful often win and the weak often weep alone. Already in 3:16 he has seen wickedness sitting “in the place of justice.” This is the Bible being unflinchingly truthful about a world you would rather sentimentalize.

For the believer, this honesty is not the end of the story, but it must be the starting place. You are not promised that the world will be fair before Christ returns. You are promised that the tears are seen — “Vengeance belongs to me; I will repay, says the Lord” (Romans 12:19) — and that a day is coming when God “will wipe away every tear from their eyes” (Revelation 21:4). Solomon himself says it in 3:17: “God will judge the righteous and the wicked.” Your tears are not unwitnessed, and your Comforter has come.

parts.label: PART TWO
parts.heading: THE RIVALRY THAT DRIVES YOU
paras: Then Solomon names the engine underneath so much striving: “I saw all the labor and achievement that is the envy of a man’s neighbor. This also is vanity and a striving after wind” (4:4). Much of what looks like ambition is really rivalry — you work not because the work is good but because you cannot bear to fall behind, and your success feeds the next man’s envy the same way his fed yours. The comparison never ends, because there is always someone ahead.

His remedy is startling in its restraint: “Better is a handful, with quietness, than two handfuls with labor and chasing after wind” (4:6). Not laziness — he condemns the fool who “folds his hands together and ruins himself” in verse 5 — but enough. One hand at rest is better than two fists clenched around more than you need, gripped so tightly by comparison that you have no peace. The dust exhausts itself trying to win a race God never entered it in.

parts.label: PART THREE
parts.heading: THE LONELINESS AT THE TOP
paras: Now Solomon paints one of the saddest portraits in the book: a man with no one. “There is one who is alone, and he has neither son nor brother. There is no end to all of his labor, neither are his eyes satisfied with wealth” (4:8). Then comes the question he finally asks himself: “For whom then, do I labor and deprive my soul of enjoyment?” He climbed all the way up and arrived utterly alone.

This is the dust’s bitterest trap: to spend your one life accumulating for an audience of none. The world can hand you wealth and power, but it cannot hand you a friend who will lift you when you fall. Only Christ meets that need — and only He teaches you to be that kind of friend to another man.

parts.label: PART FOUR
parts.heading: A CORD OF THREE STRANDS
paras: So Solomon gives the answer the whole chapter has been building toward: “Two are better than one, because they have a good reward for their labor. For if they fall, the one will lift up his fellow; but woe to him who is alone when he falls, and doesn’t have another to lift him up” (4:9–10). Two get more done together. Two can lift each other when they fall. Two can keep each other warm and stand back to back. The dust that isolates itself is the dust most easily overcome.

And then the crowning image: “a threefold cord is not quickly broken” (4:12). Two strands are stronger than one — but three hold far longer. Solomon does not name a third strand, and the verse should not be forced. But the man in Christ knows what binds his friendships from above: the Friend who “sticks closer than a brother,” who promised that nothing “will be able to separate us from God’s love which is in Christ Jesus our Lord” (Romans 8:39). The comfort the lonely world could never give, He gives, and then multiplies through the brothers He puts beside you.

stations.verse: Then I returned and saw all the oppressions that are done under the sun: and behold, the tears of those who were oppressed, and they had no comforter; and on the side of their oppressors there was power; but they had no comforter.
stations.question: How does it change your grief to know that God sees the tears the world overlooks?
stations.gloss: to comfort, to console; also to be sorry, to relent
stations.live: Bring one ache to God this week by name. Then find one man who is grieving without a comforter, and go sit with him.
body: Nacham is to comfort — to draw near to a sufferer and speak to his heart. Solomon’s lament is that under the sun the oppressed have no one to nacham them. But the same verb opens Isaiah 40: “Comfort, comfort my people,” says your God. And at the end of Genesis, Joseph comforted the brothers who had sold him and spoke kindly to them (Genesis 50:21). The comfort the fallen world withholds, God Himself supplies — and then He sends comforted men to comfort others.

stations.verse: Then I saw all the labor and achievement that is the envy of a man’s neighbor. This also is vanity and a striving after wind. The fool folds his hands together and ruins himself. Better is a handful, with quietness, than two handfuls with labor and chasing after wind.
stations.question: Where is your striving actually rivalry with another man?
stations.live: Name the man whose success stings you most. Pray for his good by name each day this week.
body: Qin’ah is heat — jealousy, envy, the burning of zeal. It can be holy: “the zeal of your house consumes me” (Psalm 69:9), a verse the disciples remembered when Jesus cleared the temple. But turned sideways toward your neighbor it becomes envy, and Proverbs says “envy rots the bones” (14:30). Solomon saw that envy sits underneath much labor and achievement. The fire is the same; the aim is what changes. Christ’s zeal was for His Father’s house, and He spent it saving you.

stations.verse: There is one who is alone, and he has neither son nor brother. There is no end to all of his labor, neither are his eyes satisfied with wealth. ‘For whom then, do I labor and deprive my soul of enjoyment?’ This also is vanity. Yes, it is a miserable business.
stations.question: For whom are you really laboring?
stations.gloss: to lack, to be without, to deprive
stations.live: This week, spend one evening fully present with the people God gave you — phone away, work closed — and thank Him for what you do not lack.
body: Chaser is to lack or to do without. The lonely man asks, “For whom then, do I labor and deprive my soul of enjoyment?” He is so bent on more that he starves himself of what he already has. Moses used the same verb for Israel in the wilderness: “you have lacked nothing” (Deuteronomy 2:7), and for the land where “you shall not lack anything” (8:9). The man who labors for no one lacks everything. The man God leads lacks nothing that matters.

stations.verse: Two are better than one, because they have a good reward for their labor. For if they fall, the one will lift up his fellow; but woe to him who is alone when he falls, and doesn’t have another to lift him up.
stations.question: Who lifts you up when you fall, and whom do you lift?
stations.live: Tell one trusted brother this week where you have fallen, and ask him to help you up. Then ask where you can do the same for him.
body: Chaver is a companion — someone joined to you. It comes from a verb meaning to unite or join together. Solomon says the one who falls has a fellow to lift him; woe to the man who falls with no one. Psalm 119:63 names the kind of companion worth having: “I am a friend of all those who fear you.” The dust was never meant to be walked alone. Christ binds you to Himself and then to His people.

stations.verse: If a man prevails against one who is alone, two shall withstand him; and a threefold cord is not quickly broken.
stations.question: What would change in one of your friendships if Christ were at the center of it?
stations.gloss: to do three times, to make threefold
stations.live: Ask one brother to meet with you weekly for a month to read Scripture and pray. Make it a cord, not a thread.
body: Shalash is the verb behind “threefold.” A cord of three strands is not quickly broken. The same word describes the three-year-old animals Abram brought when God made His covenant with him (Genesis 15:9). Solomon does not name the strands, and the verse should not be pressed further than it goes. But the picture is plain: a bond wound together holds weight that single strands cannot. Men bound to one another and to Christ do not snap under the first pull.

stations.verse: A man of many companions may be ruined, but there is a friend who sticks closer than a brother.
stations.question: What is one true friendship you could tend this week?

stations.verse: Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of mercies and God of all comfort; who comforts us in all our affliction, that we may be able to comfort those who are in any affliction, through the comfort with which we ourselves are comforted by God.
stations.question: Where has God met you in an affliction that you could now use to comfort another man?

stations.verse: He will wipe away every tear from their eyes. Death will be no more; neither will there be mourning, nor crying, nor pain, any more. The first things have passed away.’
stations.question: How does the promise of that day steady you in the injustice you face now?
pulls: The dust that isolates is the dust most easily overcome. But held by Christ and bound to His people, you are not alone.

practices.title: BRING THE INJUSTICE TO GOD
practices.body: When you see or suffer something unfair this week, resist both denial and bitterness. Take it to God, who sees every tear: “Father, this is not right, and You see it. I put the vengeance in Your hands.” Refusing to carry the injustice alone — or to avenge it yourself — is an act of trust in the Judge who will make all things right.

practices.title: TRADE RIVALRY FOR A HANDFUL OF QUIETNESS
practices.body: Notice this week where your striving is really about not falling behind someone else. When you catch the comparison, name it and lay it down: “This is rivalry, not calling.” Then deliberately choose enough over more in one concrete place.

practices.title: ASK “FOR WHOM AM I LABORING?”
practices.body: Solomon’s lonely man finally asked who it was all for. This week, ask it on purpose. Look at where your time and energy actually go, and bring it to the Son: “Jesus, am I tending the people You gave me, or only my climb?” Then take one concrete step toward a relationship you have been neglecting.

practices.title: LET THE SPIRIT MAKE YOU A COMFORTER
practices.body: You have been comforted by God in some affliction, and the Spirit wants to turn that into comfort for someone else. This week, pray: “Holy Spirit, lead me to someone weeping with no comforter, and let me bring the comfort I received.” Then watch for the man He puts in your path.

practices.title: REFUSE TO FALL ALONE
practices.body: The dust isolates; grace connects. Before the week ends, tell one trusted friend a place where you have fallen and ask him to help lift you up — and offer to be that friend for him. Do not walk this road alone when God made you for companionship.

title: No One to Comfort
subtitle: when the world is unjust and the soul is alone
keyVerse: Two are better than one, because they have a good reward for their labor. For if they fall, the one will lift up his fellow; but woe to him who is alone when he falls, and doesn’t have another to lift him up. Again, if two lie together, then they have warmth; but how can one keep warm alone? If a man prevails against one who is alone, two shall withstand him; and a threefold cord is not quickly broken.

passage.text: Moreover I saw under the sun, in the place of justice, that wickedness was there; and in the place of righteousness, that wickedness was there.
I said in my heart, “God will judge the righteous and the wicked; for there is a time there for every purpose and for every work.”
I said in my heart, “As for the sons of men, God tests them, so that they may see that they themselves are like animals.

For that which happens to the sons of men happens to animals. Even one thing happens to them. As the one dies, so the other dies. Yes, they have all one breath; and man has no advantage over the animals; for all is vanity.
All go to one place. All are from the dust, and all turn to dust again.
Who knows the spirit of man, whether it goes upward, and the spirit of the animal, whether it goes downward to the earth?”
Therefore I saw that there is nothing better than that a man should rejoice in his works; for that is his portion: for who can bring him to see what will be after him?

Then I returned and saw all the oppressions that are done under the sun: and behold, the tears of those who were oppressed, and they had no comforter; and on the side of their oppressors there was power; but they had no comforter.
Therefore I praised the dead who have been long dead more than the living who are yet alive.
Yes, better than them both is him who has not yet been, who has not seen the evil work that is done under the sun.
Then I saw all the labor and achievement that is the envy of a man’s neighbor. This also is vanity and a striving after wind.
The fool folds his hands together and ruins himself.
Better is a handful, with quietness, than two handfuls with labor and chasing after wind.
Then I returned and saw vanity under the sun.

There is one who is alone, and he has neither son nor brother. There is no end to all of his labor, neither are his eyes satisfied with wealth. “For whom then, do I labor and deprive my soul of enjoyment?” This also is vanity. Yes, it is a miserable business.
Two are better than one, because they have a good reward for their labor.
For if they fall, the one will lift up his fellow; but woe to him who is alone when he falls, and doesn’t have another to lift him up.
Again, if two lie together, then they have warmth; but how can one keep warm alone?
If a man prevails against one who is alone, two shall withstand him; and a threefold cord is not quickly broken.
Better is a poor and wise youth than an old and foolish king who doesn’t know how to receive admonition any more.
For out of prison he came out to be king; yes, even in his kingdom he was born poor.
I saw all the living who walk under the sun, that they were with the youth, the other, who succeeded him.
There was no end of all the people, even of all them over whom he was—yet those who come after shall not rejoice in him. Surely this also is vanity and a chasing after wind.

stationsLabel: THE WORD ON COMFORT AND COMPANIONSHIP
stationsIntro: Read each passage slowly, with your Bible open if you can. Do not rush to the question. Let the verse land first, then answer honestly in the lines provided — and where a Hebrew word is opened up, let it sharpen the verse you just read.
lifeTitle: Where the Ache of a Lonely World Meets Real Life
lifeIntro: This week is not about pretending the world is fair or that you are fine alone — Solomon refuses both lies. It is about receiving God’s comfort in an unjust world and letting Him bind you into the companionship you were made for.
prayer: Father, the world is unjust, and I have felt alone in it. You see every tear the world ignores. I bring mine to You. Lord Jesus, You are the Friend who sticks closer than a brother. Nothing can separate me from Your love. Holy Spirit, comfort me today, and make me a comfort to another man. Bind me to Your people. Amen.
prayerLines: Father, the world is unjust, and I have felt alone in it.
You see every tear the world ignores.
I bring mine to You.
Lord Jesus, You are the Friend who sticks closer than a brother.
Nothing can separate me from Your love.
Holy Spirit, comfort me today,
and make me a comfort to another man.
Bind me to Your people. Amen.
bottomLine: The world under the sun is unjust and lonely, and Solomon will not pretend otherwise. But the tears the world ignores are seen by the God of all comfort, and your loneliness is answered by a Friend who sticks closer than a brother. Bring both to Him, and let Him bind you to His people.
benediction: Before this week asks you to be strong, it wants you to admit two things the dust knows in its bones: the world is not fair, and it is easy to feel alone in it. Solomon looked straight at the tears of the oppressed and said the hardest part out loud — they had no comforter. He is not being bleak for effect. He is refusing to lie to you about a world where the powerful often win and the weak often weep unseen. And he is clearing the ground for a comfort that does not come from under the sun.

So lift up your eyes. When you weep and it seems no one is there, lift up your eyes — the God of all comfort sees every tear and has promised to wipe them away. When your striving becomes a lonely rivalry with no end, lift up your eyes — a handful with quietness is better than two handfuls of keeping up. When you fear you will fall with no one to lift you, lift up your eyes — there is a Friend who sticks closer than a brother, and He has put brothers around you to be His hands.

This is dust to revival, and it turns here: a soul that has stopped pretending it can face the world alone. Christ came near. He wept at a friend’s tomb, bore the judgment you deserved, and rose to bind you to Himself so that nothing can separate you from God’s love. Receive His comfort, and carry it to someone else.
closingVerse: Your tears are not unseen, and you were never meant to fall alone.
carry: Where are you carrying injustice or loneliness as if no one sees?

pulls: The dust rushes into God’s presence full of words and agenda. Wisdom draws near to listen — because God is in heaven, and that is a mercy, not a distance.
paras: For four chapters Solomon has looked outward and downward — at pleasure, wisdom, work, injustice, loneliness, all of it under the sun. Now, for a moment, he turns to the one relationship that changes everything: how a dusty soul comes before God. And his first word is not “rush in” but “slow down.” “Guard your steps when you go to God’s house.” Before you say anything to heaven, watch how you approach it.

This cuts against everything the dust assumes about God. You come to Him the way you come to everything else — hurried, full of words, full of agenda, more eager to be heard than to hear. Solomon says the opposite is wisdom: “to draw near to listen is better than to give the sacrifice of fools” (5:1). The point of coming before God is not to perform, not to inform Him, not to talk your way into His favor. It is to listen. “God is in heaven, and you on earth. Therefore let your words be few” (5:2).

Then Solomon presses into the mouth’s other danger — the vows you make and do not keep, especially the desperate promises blurted in a crisis and forgotten when it passes. Underneath both the rushing and the empty vows is the same disease: a small view of God. You would guard your steps and weigh your words if you truly grasped who it is you are approaching. “You must fear God” (5:7) — and the fear of God is not the enemy of nearness to Him. It is the doorway to it.

parts.label: PART ONE
parts.heading: DRAW NEAR TO LISTEN
paras: “Guard your steps.” Solomon is speaking of the posture of your heart as you come to God. And the first purpose of drawing near, he says, is not to talk but to listen. You so easily reverse this. You treat prayer as a speech you deliver and worship as a performance you offer, when God is inviting you into something quieter and deeper: a listening reverence that leaves its agenda at the door.

The gospel sits underneath the warning. Because of Christ, you do not guard your steps to earn access — the veil is torn, and you may “draw near with boldness to the throne of grace” (Hebrews 4:16). But boldness is not the same as carelessness. The One who tore the veil is still the God of heaven. So you come boldly and reverently, welcomed as a son yet awed by the Father, drawing near not to be heard but to hear.

parts.label: PART TWO
parts.heading: LET YOUR WORDS BE FEW
paras: “God is in heaven, and you on earth. Therefore let your words be few” (5:2). This is not a ban on prayer — Scripture calls you to pray without ceasing. It is a correction of rash words, the flood of religious talk produced to fill silence and impress heaven. “For as a dream comes with a multitude of cares, so a fool’s speech with a multitude of words” (5:3). The fool talks to feel spiritual; the wise man learns when to be quiet before God.

There is enormous relief in this if you let it land. You do not have to find the perfect words, pray the eloquent prayer, or talk long enough to be taken seriously. God is not moved by volume. “Be still, and know that I am God” (Psalm 46:10). Sometimes the most worshipful thing a dusty soul can do is stop talking, sit in the presence of the God who is in heaven, and let the fewness of its words be an act of trust that He already knows.

parts.label: PART THREE
parts.heading: KEEP WHAT YOU VOW
paras: Solomon turns to the promises made to God — often in a moment of fear or crisis, when you bargain: God, if You get me out of this, I will. “When you vow a vow to God, don’t defer to pay it; for he has no pleasure in fools. Pay that which you vow” (5:4). And then the sober counsel: “It is better that you should not vow, than that you should vow and not pay” (5:5). Better to keep silent in the crisis than to make a promise you will abandon when the danger passes.

The psalmist models the faithful pattern: “I will pay my vows to you, which my lips promised, and my mouth spoke, when I was in distress” (Psalm 66:13–14). The point is not to make you afraid to speak to God, but to make your words to Him weighty and true. A soul that guards its steps also guards its tongue — not saying to God in a panic what it will not mean when the panic lifts.

parts.label: PART FOUR
parts.heading: THE FEAR THAT FREES
paras: Solomon binds it all together: “For in the multitude of dreams there are vanities, as well as in many words; but you must fear God” (5:7). Beneath the rushing feet and the many words and the empty vows is one root problem — a God too small to fear. You would never barge into a king’s hall chattering and making promises you would not keep. You do it with God only because you have forgotten how great He is.

But the fear of God is not the opposite of nearness to God — it is the soil nearness grows in. To fear God is to see Him rightly and yourself rightly, and that clear sight is exactly what makes His welcome so astonishing. The same chapter that says “God is in heaven” also says that to rejoice in your labor “is the gift of God” (5:19). The God you rightly fear is the God who gladly gives. Guard your steps, weigh your words, keep your vows — not to earn Him, but because you have finally seen how great and how good He is.

stations.verse: Guard your steps when you go to God’s house; for to draw near to listen is better than to give the sacrifice of fools, for they don’t know that they do evil.
stations.question: When you come to God, are you mostly there to talk or to listen?
stations.gloss: to hear, to listen, to obey
stations.live: Build one stretch of silence into your time with God this week — even two minutes. Open the Word, then stop talking and listen.
body: Shama is the great listening word of the Old Testament — the first word of Israel’s confession in Deuteronomy 6:4: “Hear, Israel: Yahweh is our God. Yahweh is one.” Its range runs from hearing to heeding; to hear God rightly is to answer with your life. Solomon says the wise draw near to shama rather than to talk. And the book ends on the same word: “All has been heard” (12:13). A rushing soul that never stops to hear is, in the end, a soul not yet ready to obey.

stations.verse: Don’t be rash with your mouth, and don’t let your heart be hasty to utter anything before God; for God is in heaven, and you on earth. Therefore let your words be few.
stations.question: Where do you fill your prayers with many words to feel spiritual?
stations.gloss: to hurry, to hasten; to be hasty
stations.live: Slow your first words to God each morning this week. Say one sentence, then wait before you say another.
body: Mahar is to hurry. It can be good: Abraham “hurried into the tent” to feed his guests (Genesis 18:6). It can be ruin: Israel “soon forgot his works” (Psalm 106:13), hurrying past what God had done. Solomon warns against a heart “hasty to utter anything before God.” Hurry is not a small sin in prayer. It is a heart that thinks it has somewhere more important to be than before the God of heaven.

stations.verse: When you vow a vow to God, don’t defer to pay it; for he has no pleasure in fools. Pay that which you vow. It is better that you should not vow, than that you should vow and not pay.
stations.question: What have you promised God in a crisis that you have not kept?
stations.live: Name one promise you made to God and let slide. This week, either keep it or confess it honestly and ask for grace.
body: Neder is a vow — a promise made to God, often with an offering attached. Jacob made one at Bethel (Genesis 28:20); the psalmist paid his in the temple (Psalm 66:13). Solomon does not forbid vows. He forbids empty ones. Your whole hope rests on a God who keeps His word to you in Christ, even when you break yours to Him. That is what makes your own words worth keeping.

stations.verse: For in the multitude of dreams there are vanities, as well as in many words; but you must fear God.
stations.question: What would change in your prayers if you truly saw who you are approaching?
stations.gloss: to fear, to revere, to stand in awe
stations.live: Before you speak to God this week, pause and name who He is: the God of heaven. Let that moment of awe reset how you come.
body: Yare is the verb of holy fear — not the terror that runs from God, but the awe that comes near to Him rightly. Solomon lands this passage on it: “you must fear God.” He said the same in 3:14 — God acts so “that men should fear before him” — and he will end the whole book there: “Fear God and keep his commandments” (12:13). A soul that reveres God guards its steps, weighs its words, and keeps its vows, not out of dread, but because it has finally seen how great He is.

stations.verse: ‘Be still, and know that I am God. I will be exalted among the nations. I will be exalted in the earth.’
stations.question: Where in your hurried life do you most need to be still before God this week?
stations.gloss: to let drop, to relax, to let go
stations.live: Choose one worry you keep gripping. Each day this week, open your hands in prayer over it and say, “You will not let me drop.”
body: Raphah is to let drop or loosen your grip. In Psalm 46:10 it is the command behind “Be still”: let go, stop straining, and know that God is God. Moses used the same verb for God’s promise: “He will not fail you” (Deuteronomy 31:6) — He will not let you drop. You can loosen your grip because His does not loosen. Stillness before God is not doing nothing. It is letting go of the rope because Someone stronger is holding you.

stations.verse: Let’s therefore draw near with boldness to the throne of grace, that we may receive mercy and may find grace for help in time of need.
stations.question: How do you hold together bold access to God and the reverence Ecclesiastes calls for?

stations.verse: So, then, my beloved brothers, let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak, and slow to anger;
stations.question: Where, with God and with people, do you most need to be swift to hear this week?
pulls: You do not have to find the perfect words. God is not moved by volume. Be still, draw near to listen, and let the fewness of your words be an act of trust.

practices.title: COME TO LISTEN FIRST
practices.body: This week, flip the order of your prayers. Before you bring God your list, sit quietly and ask: “Father, what do You want to say to me?” Open the Word and let Him speak first. Coming to listen before you talk is one of the humblest, most trusting things a dusty soul can do.

practices.title: LET YOUR WORDS BE FEW
practices.body: Notice this week where your prayers become rushed or padded — many words to feel spiritual or to fill silence. Deliberately pray shorter and truer: one honest sentence instead of a paragraph of performance. God is not impressed by volume. Trust that He already knows.

practices.title: MAKE YOUR VOWS WEIGHTY
practices.body: Take stock of what you have promised God — especially anything blurted in a crisis and left unpaid. This week, bring it to Jesus honestly: either keep the vow or confess where you spoke rashly. Let your words to God be the kind you mean when the danger has passed as much as when it was near.

practices.title: ASK THE SPIRIT FOR HOLY AWE
practices.body: You cannot manufacture reverence — the Spirit gives it. Each time you come to God this week, pray first: “Holy Spirit, help me see who I am approaching, and come with awe.” Then notice how holy fear does not push you away from God but draws you nearer and makes you more honest.

practices.title: PRACTICE STILLNESS, AND SAY SO
practices.body: The dust fills every silence; grace can rest in it. Build one deliberate stretch of stillness into your time with God this week. And tell one trusted brother you are learning to draw near to listen rather than only to talk, so he can encourage you toward a quieter walk with God.

title: Guard Your Steps
subtitle: when the soul rushes into God’s presence and never stops to listen
keyVerse: Guard your steps when you go to God’s house; for to draw near to listen is better than to give the sacrifice of fools, for they don’t know that they do evil.

passage.text: Guard your steps when you go to God’s house; for to draw near to listen is better than to give the sacrifice of fools, for they don’t know that they do evil.
Don’t be rash with your mouth, and don’t let your heart be hasty to utter anything before God; for God is in heaven, and you on earth. Therefore let your words be few.
For as a dream comes with a multitude of cares, so a fool’s speech with a multitude of words.
When you vow a vow to God, don’t defer to pay it; for he has no pleasure in fools. Pay that which you vow.
It is better that you should not vow, than that you should vow and not pay.
Don’t allow your mouth to lead you into sin. Don’t protest before the messenger that this was a mistake. Why should God be angry at your voice, and destroy the work of your hands?
For in the multitude of dreams there are vanities, as well as in many words; but you must fear God.

If you see the oppression of the poor, and the violent taking away of justice and righteousness in a district, don’t marvel at the matter, for one official is eyed by a higher one, and there are officials over them.
Moreover the profit of the earth is for all. The king profits from the field.
He who loves silver shall not be satisfied with silver; nor he who loves abundance, with increase: this also is vanity.
When goods increase, those who eat them are increased; and what advantage is there to its owner, except to feast on them with his eyes?
The sleep of a laboring man is sweet, whether he eats little or much; but the abundance of the rich will not allow him to sleep.
There is a grievous evil which I have seen under the sun: wealth kept by its owner to his harm.
Those riches perish by misfortune, and if he has fathered a son, there is nothing in his hand.
As he came out of his mother’s womb, naked shall he go again as he came, and shall take nothing for his labor, which he may carry away in his hand.
This also is a grievous evil, that in all points as he came, so shall he go. And what profit does he have who labors for the wind?
All his days he also eats in darkness, he is frustrated, and has sickness and wrath.

Behold, that which I have seen to be good and proper is for one to eat and to drink, and to enjoy good in all his labor, in which he labors under the sun, all the days of his life which God has given him; for this is his portion.
Every man also to whom God has given riches and wealth, and has given him power to eat of it, and to take his portion, and to rejoice in his labor—this is the gift of God.
For he shall not often reflect on the days of his life; because God occupies him with the joy of his heart.

stationsLabel: THE WORD ON DRAWING NEAR TO GOD
stationsIntro: Read each passage slowly, with your Bible open if you can. Do not rush to the question. Let the verse land first, then answer honestly in the lines provided — and where a Hebrew word is opened up, let it sharpen the verse you just read.
lifeTitle: Where Reverence Before God Meets Real Life
lifeIntro: This week is not about becoming timid with God — Christ has given you bold access to the throne. It is about coming to Him with the reverence He deserves: guarding your steps, weighing your words, and drawing near to listen.
prayer: Father, I have rushed into Your presence full of words. You are in heaven, and I am on earth. I slow down and come to listen. Lord Jesus, You tore the veil so I could draw near. I come boldly, and I come in awe. Holy Spirit, give me a listening heart today. Teach me to fear God, and to keep the words I say to Him. Amen.
prayerLines: Father, I have rushed into Your presence full of words.
You are in heaven, and I am on earth.
I slow down and come to listen.
Lord Jesus, You tore the veil so I could draw near.
I come boldly, and I come in awe.
Holy Spirit, give me a listening heart today.
Teach me to fear God,
and to keep the words I say to Him. Amen.
bottomLine: The dust rushes into God’s presence full of words, agenda, and rash promises, because it has forgotten how great He is. Wisdom guards its steps, lets its words be few, keeps its vows, and draws near to listen. The fear of God is not the enemy of nearness to Him; it is the soil nearness grows in.
benediction: Before this week asks you to speak to God, it wants to teach you how to approach Him. Solomon, who chased everything under the sun, finally turns toward heaven — and his first counsel is not “rush in” but “guard your steps.” Draw near to listen. Let your words be few. Keep your vows. Underneath all of it is one recovered truth: God is in heaven and you are on earth, and that distance is not coldness — it is greatness, the very greatness that makes His welcome a wonder.

So lift up your eyes. When you come to God hurried and full of words, lift up your eyes — He is in heaven, and the wise soul draws near to listen. When you have made promises to Him you did not keep, lift up your eyes — bring them back honestly to the God who keeps every promise He makes. When reverence feels like distance, lift up your eyes — the fear of God is not the wall between you and Him; it is the doorway into knowing Him.

This is dust to revival, and it turns here: a soul that has stopped barging in and started bowing low. The veil was torn when Christ died, and the throne you approach is a throne of grace. Come near. Come in awe. Come to listen.
closingVerse: The fear of God is not the wall between you and Him. It is the doorway into knowing Him.
carry: Where do you rush into God’s presence instead of drawing near to listen?

pulls: You can have more of everything and still starve at the table. The soul that nothing under the sun can fill was built for the One above it.
paras: There is an evil under the sun that Solomon says is heavy on men, and it is one of the strangest and saddest things in the book: a man who has everything and cannot enjoy any of it. God gives him “riches, wealth, and honor, so that he lacks nothing for his soul of all that he desires, yet God gives him no power to eat of it, but an alien eats it” (6:2). Full hands, empty heart. The table is loaded, and he has no appetite for the feast. If you have ever gotten exactly what you wanted and felt nothing, you have tasted this evil.

Solomon presses the point past comfort. A man could father a hundred children and live many years — even “a thousand years twice told” — and still, if “his soul is not filled with good,” then “a stillborn child is better than he” (6:3–6). It is a shocking thing to say, and he means it to shock. Length of life, size of family, weight of wealth — none of them can manufacture a satisfied soul. You can have more of everything and still be a starving man at a full table.

Then he names the ache in one unforgettable line: “All the labor of man is for his mouth, and yet the appetite is not filled” (6:7). You spend your whole life feeding a hunger that will not stay fed. The mouth is filled and the appetite returns; the desire is met and it simply relocates. This is not a design flaw — it is a signpost. The soul that cannot be satisfied by anything under the sun is a soul built for Someone above it. The power to eat and rejoice, Solomon has already said, “is the gift of God” (5:19) — and a gift must be received from the Giver, not seized from the things themselves.

parts.label: PART ONE
parts.heading: FULL HANDS, EMPTY HEART
paras: Solomon draws a hard line between having and enjoying, and he insists they are two different gifts. A man can accumulate everything his eyes desire and still lack the one thing that would make it worth anything: the God-given power to actually eat of it. He labors his whole life to fill the barn, and “an alien eats it” (6:2).

This should stop you cold, because your whole culture is built on the assumption that having is enjoying — that if you could just acquire enough, the satisfaction would follow automatically. Solomon says no. The wealth is real; the enjoyment is a separate gift, and it comes only from God’s hand. You can be rich in possessions and bankrupt in joy. And no amount of the first will ever purchase the second.

parts.label: PART TWO
parts.heading: MORE IS NOT THE ANSWER
paras: Then Solomon dismantles your last defense — the quiet belief that you are just one increment short. Surely more children, more years, more security would finally satisfy. So he takes the argument to its extreme: a hundred children, two thousand years. And still, if the soul is not filled with good, a stillborn child is better off (6:3–6). He is not being cruel; he is being merciful, killing the lie before it kills you.

The lie is more. It whispers that dissatisfaction is a math problem — add enough and the ache resolves. Solomon proves it is not a math problem at all. “Don’t all go to one place?” (6:6). More does not change the destination and it does not fill the soul. If length and abundance cannot satisfy, then satisfaction was never a quantity to accumulate. It is a gift to receive.

parts.label: PART THREE
parts.heading: THE APPETITE THAT RELOCATES
paras: “All the labor of man is for his mouth, and yet the appetite is not filled” (6:7). The machinery of the whole book lies bare. You labor to feed a hunger; the hunger is fed; the hunger returns. “Better is the sight of the eyes than the wandering of the desire” (6:9) — better to be content with what is in front of you than to keep chasing the desire that always moves on. But how? The appetite is relentless, and everything under the sun is only a temporary meal.

The relentlessness is the point. An appetite that nothing can permanently satisfy is either a curse or a compass. If there is no God, it is a cruel joke — an endless hunger with no possible meal. But if you were made for God, the hunger is holy: it will not let you settle for less than Him. “For he satisfies the longing soul. He fills the hungry soul with good” (Psalm 107:9). The appetite was never meant to be fed by things. It was meant to drive you to the One who fills it.

parts.label: PART FOUR
parts.heading: THE BREAD THAT SATISFIES
paras: So Solomon leaves you hungry on purpose — and centuries later a Man says the sentence Ecclesiastes has been aching toward: “I am the bread of life. Whoever comes to me will not be hungry, and whoever believes in me will never be thirsty” (John 6:35). The appetite that no wealth, no family, no length of years could satisfy meets, at last, the only meal that fills it. Not a thing to acquire, but a Person to receive.

This is the answer to the evil under the sun. The problem was never that you had too little; it was that you kept going to the things instead of the Giver. Jesus does not offer to help you accumulate more — He offers to be the satisfaction you were chasing all along. “Whoever drinks of the water that I will give him will never thirst again” (John 4:14). The dust does not need a bigger barn. It needs the Bread of Life.

stations.verse: There is an evil which I have seen under the sun, and it is heavy on men: a man to whom God gives riches, wealth, and honor, so that he lacks nothing for his soul of all that he desires, yet God gives him no power to eat of it, but an alien eats it. This is vanity, and it is an evil disease.
stations.question: What good thing is in your hands right now that you cannot seem to enjoy?
stations.live: List three things you own that you have stopped enjoying. Thank God for each by name, and give one of them away or put it to use for someone else.
body: Osher is plain wealth — riches you can count. Solomon says God can give a man osher and still withhold the power to eat of it. In 5:13 he saw “wealth kept by its owner to his harm.” Psalm 52:7 describes the man who “trusted in the abundance of his riches” instead of making God his strength. Riches are not evil. They are simply not a strength. The only riches that hold are the ones Christ gives.

stations.verse: If a man fathers a hundred children, and lives many years, so that the days of his years are many, but his soul is not filled with good, and moreover he has no burial; I say, that a stillborn child is better than he:
stations.question: What would it mean to measure your life by whether your soul is filled with good rather than by how much you have?
stations.live: Think honestly this week about your own burial. Then read Matthew 28:1–6 and thank Christ for the tomb that could not hold Him.
body: Qevurah is burial — the grave and the honor of being laid in it. Solomon’s rich man has a hundred children and “no burial.” Jacob asked to be carried out of Egypt and laid in his fathers’ burying place (Genesis 47:30); the proud king of Isaiah 14 is denied burial altogether. A man can gain everything and still be thrown out at the end. Christ was laid in a borrowed tomb, and He did not stay there. His grave is the only one that became a door.

stations.verse: All the labor of man is for his mouth, and yet the appetite is not filled.
stations.question: Where do you keep feeding an appetite that simply returns hungrier?
stations.live: When your soul cries for the next thing this week, answer it out loud: “You were made for the living God — not this.”
body: Nephesh is the living self — soul, life, and appetite in one word. In 6:7 WEB renders it “appetite”; in 6:2 it is the “soul” that lacks nothing; in 2:24 it is the soul a man makes to “enjoy good in his labor.” The same hungering self runs through all three. The tragedy of Ecclesiastes 6 is a nephesh fed everything under the sun and still starving. The hope of the gospel is a nephesh brought to the only One who can fill it.

stations.verse: Better is the sight of the eyes than the wandering of the desire. This also is vanity and a chasing after wind.
stations.question: What good gift are you overlooking while your desire wanders after the next thing?
stations.live: Each evening this week, write down one good thing you saw that day and did not have to chase.
body: Mar’eh is sight — what is in front of your eyes. “Better is the sight of the eyes than the wandering of the desire.” The phrase is homely and exact: better to enjoy what you can see than to chase what you can only imagine. The same word describes the trees in Eden, “pleasant to the sight” (Genesis 2:9). Man had every good thing in view and reached for the one thing forbidden. Contentment is learning to see the good God has already set in front of you.

stations.verse: Jesus said to them, ‘I am the bread of life. Whoever comes to me will not be hungry, and whoever believes in me will never be thirsty.
stations.question: Where are you still going to the world’s table for a fullness only the Bread of Life can give?

stations.verse: Let them praise Yahweh for his loving kindness, for his wonderful deeds to the children of men! For he satisfies the longing soul. He fills the hungry soul with good.
stations.question: Where do you need to stop striving to fill yourself and simply come to God hungry this week?
stations.gloss: to run about, to rush; to be eager, to long
stations.live: Name the thing you keep running back to. This week, when you feel the pull, stop and pray Psalm 107:9 before you move.
body: Shaqaq describes something rushing about — eager, craving, restless. God “satisfies the longing soul,” the soul that runs back and forth looking for water. Isaiah 29:8 uses the same verb for a man who dreams he drinks and wakes still faint with thirst. That is every appetite fed under the sun: you dream you are full, and you wake up dry. Only God fills the longing soul with good.

stations.verse: My God will supply every need of yours according to his riches in glory in Christ Jesus.
stations.question: Where are you anxiously accumulating what God has already promised to supply?
pulls: The appetite that nothing under the sun can fill is not a curse. It is a compass, made to drive you to the Bread of Life.

practices.title: SEPARATE HAVING FROM ENJOYING
practices.body: This week, notice the good things already in your hands that you are failing to enjoy — rushing past, taking for granted, unable to savor. Name one, and ask God for the gift He alone gives: “Father, give me the power to actually enjoy this, received from Your hand.” Enjoyment is not automatic; it is grace. Ask for it.

practices.title: STOP BELIEVING THE LIE OF “MORE”
practices.body: Catch the whisper this week that says your dissatisfaction is just one increment short — one more purchase, achievement, or change away from being content. Name it as the lie Solomon exposed: “More is not the answer.” Then choose contentment with what is in front of you in one concrete place.

practices.title: BRING YOUR HUNGER TO THE SON
practices.body: When the deep appetite cries out this week — for more, for the next thing, for the fullness you cannot name — do not just feed it and do not just resist it. Bring it to Jesus: “You are the Bread of Life. I come to You hungry.” Let the craving drive you to the only meal that satisfies.

practices.title: ASK THE SPIRIT FOR CONTENTMENT
practices.body: A satisfied soul is not a personality trait you can force — it is a gift the Spirit grows. Each morning this week, pray: “Holy Spirit, teach me to be filled by Christ today, so I stop asking things to do what only He can do.” Then watch for the moments the grasping quiets.

practices.title: FEED SOMEONE ELSE’S HUNGER
practices.body: The dust hoards to fill itself; grace gives. This week, meet a real need in someone else — a meal, a kindness, a provision. And tell one trusted brother the hunger you have been trying to feed under the sun, so he can help you carry it to Christ.

title: The Soul Never Filled
subtitle: when you have everything and cannot enjoy any of it
keyVerse: All the labor of man is for his mouth, and yet the appetite is not filled.

passage.text: There is an evil which I have seen under the sun, and it is heavy on men:

a man to whom God gives riches, wealth, and honor, so that he lacks nothing for his soul of all that he desires, yet God gives him no power to eat of it, but an alien eats it. This is vanity, and it is an evil disease.

If a man fathers a hundred children, and lives many years, so that the days of his years are many, but his soul is not filled with good, and moreover he has no burial; I say, that a stillborn child is better than he:
for it comes in vanity, and departs in darkness, and its name is covered with darkness.
Moreover it has not seen the sun nor known it. This has rest rather than the other.
Yes, though he live a thousand years twice told, and yet fails to enjoy good, don’t all go to one place?
All the labor of man is for his mouth, and yet the appetite is not filled.
For what advantage has the wise more than the fool? What has the poor man, that knows how to walk before the living?
Better is the sight of the eyes than the wandering of the desire. This also is vanity and a chasing after wind.
Whatever has been, its name was given long ago; and it is known what man is; neither can he contend with him who is mightier than he.
For there are many words that create vanity. What does that profit man?
For who knows what is good for man in life, all the days of his vain life which he spends like a shadow? For who can tell a man what will be after him under the sun?

stationsLabel: THE WORD ON THE UNSATISFIED SOUL
stationsIntro: Read each passage slowly, with your Bible open if you can. Do not rush to the question. Let the verse land first, then answer honestly in the lines provided — and where a Hebrew word is opened up, let it sharpen the verse you just read.
lifeTitle: Where the Unsatisfied Soul Meets Real Life
lifeIntro: This week is not about wanting less or numbing your desires — it is about bringing your real hunger to the only One who can fill it. The power to enjoy your life is a gift from God’s hand, received in coming to Christ.
prayer: Father, I have tried to fill my soul with things under the sun. My hands are full, and my heart is still hungry. I come to You hungry. Lord Jesus, You are the Bread of Life. Whoever comes to You will not be hungry. I come. Holy Spirit, give me the power to enjoy God’s gifts and to be satisfied in Christ today. Amen.
prayerLines: Father, I have tried to fill my soul with things under the sun.
My hands are full, and my heart is still hungry.
I come to You hungry.
Lord Jesus, You are the Bread of Life.
Whoever comes to You will not be hungry.
I come.
Holy Spirit, give me the power to enjoy God’s gifts
and to be satisfied in Christ today. Amen.
bottomLine: You can have everything under the sun and still starve at the table, because having is not enjoying and more is not the answer. The appetite nothing could fill was built to drive you to the Bread of Life. Bring your real hunger to Christ.
benediction: Before this week asks you to be content, it wants you to face the evil Solomon saw: a soul with full hands and an empty heart, a man at a loaded table with no power to eat. You have felt the edge of it — the thing you finally got that gave you nothing, the ache that returned the morning after you had everything you thought you wanted. Solomon is not being bleak. He is refusing to let you keep believing that having is enjoying, or that more will ever be enough.

So lift up your eyes. When you cannot enjoy the good already in your hands, lift up your eyes — the power to enjoy your life is a gift from God’s hand, and He gives it. When the lie of more whispers that you are one increment from satisfied, lift up your eyes — all go to one place, and the soul does not fill by accumulation. When your appetite returns hungrier no matter how you feed it, lift up your eyes — that hunger was a compass all along, pointing to the Bread of Life.

This is dust to revival, and it turns here: a soul that has stopped trying to fill itself from the world’s table. Christ gave His body as bread for the life of the world. Whoever comes to Him will not be hungry, and whoever believes in Him will never be thirsty. Come hungry, and be filled.
closingVerse: You were never going to fill your soul from the world’s table. Come hungry to the Bread of Life.
carry: What hunger are you still trying to satisfy with something under the sun?

pulls: The fool changes the subject; the wise man sits with it. Settle your eternity, and let the house of mourning make you wise.
paras: Solomon says something in chapter seven that a comfort-loving age finds almost impossible to hear: “It is better to go to the house of mourning than to go to the house of feasting.” He is not a gloomy man who prefers funerals to parties. He is a wise man telling you where wisdom is actually learned — and it is not where the music is loudest. It is at the graveside, where “the living should take this to heart,” where a soul finally stops pretending it will live forever and starts asking what its one life is for.

This is the dust getting honest about the thing it works hardest to avoid: its own end. The day of death is “better than the day of one’s birth” (7:1), Solomon says — not because death is good, but because a funeral tells the truth a party cannot. A birthday celebrates potential; a funeral reveals a life. And the mourner, standing in that room, is quietly forced to reckon with the fact that his day is coming too. “The heart of the wise is in the house of mourning; but the heart of fools is in the house of mirth” (7:4). The fool changes the subject. The wise man sits with it.

Why does Solomon aim you at sorrow? Because “by the sadness of the face the heart is made good” (7:3) — there is a grief that does the soul good, a mourning that clears the eyes. It is hard to face eternity while your own eternity is unsettled, and the house of mourning presses that question in a way the house of feasting never will. This is not morbid. It is the mercy of a wise man handing you a mirror and saying: look, while you still have breath. The soul that faces death rightly is the soul most ready to live — and most ready to lift its eyes to the only One who conquered it.

parts.label: PART ONE
parts.heading: WHERE WISDOM IS LEARNED
paras: Solomon flips your instincts upside down. You run toward the feast and away from the funeral, and he says the funeral has more to teach. A death day reveals more about a man than his birthday ever could: it shows what the life amounted to, what it was built on, what it left behind. Stand in that room and you cannot help but measure your own life against the same yardstick.

This is not the Bible glorifying misery. It is the Bible refusing to let you numb yourself against the one certainty that should shape every other choice. “So teach us to count our days, that we may gain a heart of wisdom” (Psalm 90:12). Wisdom is not learned by pretending death is far off; it is learned by facing it squarely and letting that clear-eyed reckoning reorder how you spend the breath you have left.

parts.label: PART TWO
parts.heading: THE GRIEF THAT HEALS
paras: “Sorrow is better than laughter; for by the sadness of the face the heart is made good” (7:3). Solomon is not against joy — he is against the shallow laughter that dodges reality. “For as the crackling of thorns under a pot, so is the laughter of the fool” (7:6): a lot of noise and heat, gone in a moment, cooking nothing. The fool laughs to avoid; the wise man grieves to grow.

There is a kind of sadness that does the soul good — the sorrow that comes from seeing clearly, that softens a hard heart and turns it toward God. Paul says, “godly sorrow produces repentance to salvation, which brings no regret” (2 Corinthians 7:10). The dust would rather drown its ache in noise. But the tears that clear the eyes are worth more than the laughter that numbs them. Do not run from every sorrow. Some of it is the very thing God is using to make your heart good.

parts.label: PART THREE
parts.heading: PATIENCE OVER PRIDE
paras: Solomon turns from mortality to the daily posture of a wise heart, and it is startlingly practical. “Better is the end of a thing than its beginning. The patient in spirit is better than the proud in spirit” (7:8). The dust wants results now and takes offense fast. Wisdom waits to see how the story ends and refuses to let anger set up house in its chest: “Don’t be hasty in your spirit to be angry, for anger rests in the bosom of fools” (7:9).

And he names one of your favorite foolish habits: nostalgia. “Don’t say, ‘Why were the former days better than these?’ For you do not ask wisely about this” (7:10). The fool is always sure the good days are behind him, romanticizing a past that was never as golden as memory paints it. The wise man receives today — this actual day God has given — as the place to walk with Him, neither anxious about tomorrow nor pining for a yesterday that is gone.

parts.label: PART FOUR
parts.heading: CONSIDER THE WORK OF GOD
paras: Solomon lands the passage on trust: “Consider the work of God, for who can make that straight, which he has made crooked?” (7:13). You have met this crooked line before — the twists in life that no human wisdom can untwist. Here his counsel is not despair but surrender: stop trying to straighten what only God can straighten, and consider His work, trusting that the hand behind the crooked places is wise and good.

“In the day of prosperity be joyful, and in the day of adversity consider; yes, God has made the one side by side with the other” (7:14). Both the good day and the hard day come from His hand. The wise heart holds them both — receiving prosperity with gladness and meeting adversity with reflection, refusing to demand explanations God has not given. And the crooked thing wisdom could never straighten, Christ took to a cross, turning the last house of mourning — a tomb — into the doorway of resurrection. The soul that considers the work of God can trust it, even in the dark, because it has seen what He did with a grave.

stations.verse: It is better to go to the house of mourning than to go to the house of feasting; for that is the end of all men, and the living should take this to heart.
stations.question: Where do you avoid the house of mourning by refusing to think about your own end?
stations.live: Attend the next funeral or visit the next grieving family you can this week, and let it teach you. Pray Isaiah 61:3 over that family.
body: Evel is mourning — the grief of a funeral and the days of lament after it. Joseph mourned his father seven days at the threshing floor of Atad (Genesis 50:10). Solomon says the house of evel is where wisdom is learned. And Isaiah 61:3 promises what only God can do: “the oil of joy for mourning.” Jesus read from that very chapter in Nazareth and said it was fulfilled in Him. The house of mourning is not the last house.

stations.verse: Sorrow is better than laughter; for by the sadness of the face the heart is made good.
stations.question: What sorrow have you been drowning in noise instead of letting God use it?
stations.gloss: to be good, to go well, to make good
stations.live: Name one grief you have tried to outrun. Sit with it before God for ten minutes this week, and ask Him to use it to make your heart good.
body: Yatav is to be good or to go well. By sadness of face, Solomon says, the heart is “made good.” The verb is the same one God used with Cain: “If you do well” (Genesis 4:7). Sorrow is not the goal. It is a tool in God’s hand for making a hard heart good. The world treats every grief as a malfunction to fix. God sometimes uses grief to do what comfort never could.

stations.verse: Better is the end of a thing than its beginning. The patient in spirit is better than the proud in spirit. Don’t be hasty in your spirit to be angry, for anger rests in the bosom of fools.
stations.question: What would patience in spirit look like in the situation that most tests you this week?
stations.live: When you feel anger rise this week, pray Psalm 103:8 before you answer. Remember how long God has been patient with you.
body: Erekh means long — and with “spirit” or “anger,” long-suffering, slow to boil. “The patient in spirit is better than the proud in spirit.” Its most famous use is about God Himself: “Yahweh is merciful and gracious, slow to anger” (Psalm 103:8). Your patience is not a technique. It is a reflection of the God who has been patient with you. Every time He did not give you what you deserved, erekh was at work.

stations.verse: Don’t say, ‘Why were the former days better than these?’ For you do not ask wisely about this.
