stations.question: What are you missing right now because you keep looking back at the former days?

stations.verse: Wisdom is as good as an inheritance. Yes, it is more excellent for those who see the sun. For wisdom is a defense, even as money is a defense; but the excellency of knowledge is that wisdom preserves the life of him who has it.
stations.question: What does it mean for you to take shelter in God’s wisdom this week instead of in your money?
stations.live: Pray Psalm 91:1 each morning this week. When money worries rise, name where your real shelter is.
body: Tsel is shadow — shade from the sun, and so shelter. WEB renders 7:12 “wisdom is a defense, even as money is a defense,” but the Hebrew picture is shade: to be “in the shadow” of wisdom or of money. Solomon also uses tsel for life itself, spent “like a shadow” (6:12). Money gives a thin shade that moves with the sun. The psalmist names the shade that holds: “He who dwells in the secret place of the Most High will rest in the shadow of the Almighty” (Psalm 91:1).

stations.verse: So teach us to count our days, that we may gain a heart of wisdom.
stations.question: If you truly counted your days as limited, what would you do differently with the ones you have left?

stations.verse: For godly sorrow produces repentance to salvation, which brings no regret. But the sorrow of the world produces death.
stations.question: Where do you need to let a sorrow turn you toward God rather than away from Him?
stations.live: Bring one sin you grieve to Christ this week and confess it plainly. Then thank Him that godly sorrow ends in joy.
body: Lupē is grief — pain of heart. Paul names two kinds: godly sorrow that produces repentance and brings no regret, and the sorrow of the world that produces death. The difference is not how much it hurts, but where it turns you. Jesus used the same word the night before the cross: “your sorrow will be turned into joy” (John 16:20). Three days later it was. Godly lupē is sorrow with a resurrection at the end of it.
pulls: Wisdom is learned at the graveside, not the party. Count your days, take the truth to heart, and trust the God who emptied a tomb.

practices.title: COUNT YOUR DAYS ON PURPOSE
practices.body: This week, deliberately do the thing the fool avoids: consider your own mortality before God. Not morbidly — wisely. Ask, “If my days are truly numbered, what am I spending them on that will not matter, and what am I neglecting that will?” Let that honest reckoning reorder one concrete thing about how you use this week.

practices.title: LET SORROW DO ITS WORK
practices.body: When a sadness comes this week, resist the urge to immediately drown it in noise or distraction. Sit with it before God long enough to ask what it is teaching you. Some sorrow is godly — the very thing softening your heart and turning it toward Him. Do not numb every ache.

practices.title: CHOOSE PATIENCE OVER PRIDE
practices.body: Notice this week where you demand results now and take offense fast. When the anger or impatience rises, bring it to Jesus: “Lord, I am proud and hurried here. Give me a patient spirit that waits to see the end.” The patient heart trusts that Christ is writing a better ending than your impatience can imagine.

practices.title: ASK THE SPIRIT TO KEEP YOU IN TODAY
practices.body: The fool pines for the former days or frets about tomorrow. Each morning this week, pray: “Holy Spirit, keep me in this day — the one God actually gave me.” Then receive today as the place to walk with God, and give the rest to Him.

practices.title: CONSIDER THE WORK OF GOD WITH A BROTHER
practices.body: When you hit a crooked thing this week that you cannot straighten, stop wrestling it alone. Consider the work of God, trust the hand behind it, and tell one trusted brother the situation you are learning to surrender rather than fix. Let him remind you what God did with the crookedest thing of all: He turned a tomb into a doorway.

title: The House of Mourning
subtitle: when facing death is the wisest thing a soul can do
keyVerse: It is better to go to the house of mourning than to go to the house of feasting; for that is the end of all men, and the living should take this to heart.

passage.text: A good name is better than fine perfume; and the day of death better than the day of one’s birth.
It is better to go to the house of mourning than to go to the house of feasting; for that is the end of all men, and the living should take this to heart.
Sorrow is better than laughter; for by the sadness of the face the heart is made good.
The heart of the wise is in the house of mourning; but the heart of fools is in the house of mirth.
It is better to hear the rebuke of the wise than for a man to hear the song of fools.
For as the crackling of thorns under a pot, so is the laughter of the fool. This also is vanity.
Surely extortion makes the wise man foolish; and a bribe destroys the understanding.
Better is the end of a thing than its beginning. The patient in spirit is better than the proud in spirit.
Don’t be hasty in your spirit to be angry, for anger rests in the bosom of fools.
Don’t say, “Why were the former days better than these?” For you do not ask wisely about this.
Wisdom is as good as an inheritance. Yes, it is more excellent for those who see the sun.
For wisdom is a defense, even as money is a defense; but the excellency of knowledge is that wisdom preserves the life of him who has it.
Consider the work of God, for who can make that straight, which he has made crooked?
In the day of prosperity be joyful, and in the day of adversity consider; yes, God has made the one side by side with the other, to the end that man should not find out anything after him.
All this I have seen in my days of vanity: there is a righteous man who perishes in his righteousness, and there is a wicked man who lives long in his evildoing.
Don’t be overly righteous, neither make yourself overly wise. Why should you destroy yourself?
Don’t be too wicked, neither be foolish. Why should you die before your time?
It is good that you should take hold of this. Yes, also don’t withdraw your hand from that; for he who fears God will come out of them all.
Wisdom is a strength to the wise man more than ten rulers who are in a city.
Surely there is not a righteous man on earth who does good and doesn’t sin.
Also don’t take heed to all words that are spoken, lest you hear your servant curse you;
for often your own heart knows that you yourself have likewise cursed others.
All this I have proved in wisdom. I said, “I will be wise;” but it was far from me.
That which is, is far off and exceedingly deep. Who can find it out?
I turned around, and my heart sought to know and to search out, and to seek wisdom and the scheme of things, and to know that wickedness is stupidity, and that foolishness is madness.
I find more bitter than death the woman whose heart is snares and traps, whose hands are chains. Whoever pleases God shall escape from her; but the sinner will be ensnared by her.
“Behold, I have found this,” says the Preacher, “to one another, to find out the scheme
which my soul still seeks, but I have not found. I have found one man among a thousand, but I have not found a woman among all those.
Behold, I have only found this: that God made man upright; but they search for many schemes.”

stationsLabel: THE WORD ON THE WISE HEART
stationsIntro: Read each passage slowly, with your Bible open if you can. Do not rush to the question. Let the verse land first, then answer honestly in the lines provided — and where a Hebrew or Greek word is opened up, let it sharpen the verse you just read.
lifeTitle: Where the Wise Heart Meets Real Life
lifeIntro: This week is not a call to gloom — Solomon commends joy in the day of prosperity. It is a call to face reality with a wise heart: to count your days, let honest sorrow do its work, and trust the God behind both the good day and the hard one.
prayer: Father, teach me to count my days. I have run from the house of mourning and hidden in noise. Lord Jesus, You wept at a grave, and You walked out of Your own. I trust You with what I cannot straighten. Holy Spirit, keep me in today, patient and clear-eyed before God. Amen.
prayerLines: Father, teach me to count my days.
I have run from the house of mourning
and hidden in noise.
Lord Jesus, You wept at a grave,
and You walked out of Your own.
I trust You with what I cannot straighten.
Holy Spirit, keep me in today,
patient and clear-eyed before God. Amen.
bottomLine: Wisdom is learned at the graveside, where the living take it to heart. The wise man counts his days, lets honest sorrow soften him, chooses patience over pride, and trusts the God behind both the good day and the hard one. The One who emptied a tomb can be trusted with everything you cannot straighten.
benediction: Before this week hands you comfort, it hands you a mirror. Solomon says the wise heart is found in the house of mourning, not the house of mirth — not because sorrow is the goal, but because the graveside tells a truth the party never will. There, with the living taking it to heart, a soul finally stops pretending it will live forever and starts asking what its one life is for. That is not morbid. It is the beginning of wisdom, and the dust avoids it at its peril.

So lift up your eyes. When you are tempted to dodge every hard reality with noise, lift up your eyes — there is a grief that clears the eyes and a God who makes the sad heart good. When you are proud and impatient and sure the good days are behind you, lift up your eyes — the end of a thing is better than its beginning, and He is writing the end. When you hit a crooked thing you cannot straighten, lift up your eyes — consider the work of God, who took the crookedest thing of all to a cross.

This is dust to revival, and it turns here: a soul that has stopped avoiding its own mortality. Jesus stood at a tomb and said, “I am the resurrection and the life.” Then He went into His own and came out on the third day. The last house of mourning has already been emptied.
closingVerse: The wise face death and grow ready to live. The tomb is already empty.
carry: Where are you dodging the reality of your own mortality?

pulls: The two things you most want to control — what is coming and when it ends — God keeps in His own hands. That is not helplessness. That is an invitation to trust.
paras: The wisest man who ever lived reaches, at the end of chapter eight, a confession that would humble anyone: “man can’t find out the work that is done under the sun.” Solomon, who once asked God for an understanding heart and received wisdom beyond every king before him, admits there is a limit even his mind cannot cross. “Even though a wise man thinks he can comprehend it, he won’t be able to find it” (8:17). The dust wants to figure everything out — to see the future, to trace the pattern, to understand why. Solomon, from the summit of human understanding, tells you plainly: you cannot.

Two things in particular lie beyond your reach. First, the future: “For he doesn’t know that which will be; for who can tell him how it will be?” (8:7). You do not know what tomorrow holds, and no amount of planning, worrying, or wisdom will pull the veil back. Second, the day of your death: “neither does he have power over the day of death” (8:8). The two things you most want to control — what is coming and when it ends — are precisely the things God has kept in His own hands.

This could be a terror or a rest, and the difference is entirely a matter of whom you believe holds what you cannot see. To a soul under the sun, “you cannot know the future” is a nightmare of helplessness. But to a soul that has lifted its eyes, it is an invitation to trust: the future you cannot discover is fully known to the God who holds it, and the day of death you cannot control is already written in His book. Solomon’s dead end is God’s open door. You were never meant to find it out. You were meant to trust Him.

parts.label: PART ONE
parts.heading: THE LIMITS OF THE WISEST MIND
paras: Solomon opens with the value of wisdom — “A man’s wisdom makes his face shine” (8:1) — and then spends the chapter marking its borders. He counsels wisdom in dealing with kings, saying the wise heart “will know the time and procedure” (8:5). But even the wise heart that knows the right time for things runs headlong into what it cannot know: “For he doesn’t know that which will be” (8:7).

This is a needed humbling. You assume that with enough intelligence, information, and planning, you could master your life — anticipate every outcome, control every variable. Solomon, who had more wisdom than you will ever possess, says flatly that the future is closed to human sight. The smartest plan in the world cannot tell you what next week holds. Wisdom is real and good, but it has a wall, and the wall is tomorrow.

parts.label: PART TWO
parts.heading: WHEN JUSTICE SEEMS DELAYED
paras: Then Solomon presses into one of faith’s hardest tests: a world where the wicked seem to get away with it. “Because sentence against an evil work is not executed speedily, therefore the heart of the sons of men is fully set in them to do evil” (8:11). When judgment is delayed, men conclude it will never come — and evil grows bold. He even sees “righteous men to whom it happens according to the work of the wicked” (8:14). The good suffer; the guilty prosper. It looks upside down.

But watch the anchor Solomon drops in the middle of the confusion: “yet surely I know that it will be better with those who fear God” and “it shall not be well with the wicked” (8:12–13). He cannot explain the timing, and he refuses to pretend the injustice is not real — but he holds fast to what he does know: God sees, God will judge, and in the end it will be well with those who fear Him. The delay is not denial. A sentence not yet executed is not a sentence forgotten.

parts.label: PART THREE
parts.heading: ENOUGH FOR TODAY
paras: Having stared at the future he cannot see, Solomon does something surprising: he commends ordinary, God-given joy. “Then I commended mirth, because a man has no better thing under the sun, than to eat, and to drink, and to be joyful: for that will accompany him in his labor all the days of his life which God has given him under the sun” (8:15). This is not surrender to pleasure-seeking — it is the freedom of a soul that has stopped demanding to control tomorrow and learned to receive today as a gift.

This is exactly where Jesus lands you: “Therefore don’t be anxious for tomorrow, for tomorrow will be anxious for itself. Each day’s own evil is sufficient” (Matthew 6:34). God has not given you tomorrow’s knowledge because He has not given you tomorrow yet — only today. And today He gives enough: enough grace, enough bread, enough of Himself. The dust exhausts itself trying to live in a future it cannot enter. Wisdom receives the day it has been given and trusts the God who holds the rest.

parts.label: PART FOUR
parts.heading: TRUSTING THE GOD YOU CANNOT TRACE
paras: So Solomon’s conclusion is not despair but surrender: man “can’t find out the work that is done under the sun” (8:17). And that confession, far from crushing faith, is where faith finally breathes. You do not have to understand the work of God to trust the God who is working. “For my thoughts are not your thoughts, and your ways are not my ways,” says Yahweh (Isaiah 55:8). What you cannot discover is not a locked door slammed in your face; it is the wise providence of a Father too great to fit inside your understanding.

This is the deepest rest the book has offered yet. The very thing that terrifies the soul under the sun — I cannot see, I cannot control, I cannot understand — becomes, for the soul that lifts its eyes, the ground of peace: but He can, and He does, and He is good. “All things work together for good for those who love God” (Romans 8:28), even the things you will never trace. You will not discover the pattern. But you can trust the One weaving it — the same One who worked His deepest purpose through a cross that looked, at the time, like the triumph of injustice itself.

stations.verse: For he doesn’t know that which will be; for who can tell him how it will be?
stations.question: Where are you exhausting yourself trying to know a future God has kept hidden?
stations.gloss: to tell, to make known, to declare
stations.live: When you catch yourself rehearsing tomorrow this week, stop and say out loud one thing God has already told you in His Word.
body: Nagad is to tell — to make something known that was hidden. “Who can tell him how it will be?” No one. Solomon asks it again in 10:14: “that which will be after him, who can tell him?” The first time the verb shows up in the Bible, God asks Adam, “Who told you that you were naked?” (Genesis 3:11). Man grasped at knowledge and found shame. God does not tell you tomorrow. He has told you something better: what He did for you in Christ.

stations.verse: Because sentence against an evil work is not executed speedily, therefore the heart of the sons of men is fully set in them to do evil. Though a sinner commits crimes a hundred times, and lives long, yet surely I know that it will be better with those who fear God, who are reverent before him.
stations.question: Where does the delay of God’s justice tempt you to doubt it will come at all?
stations.live: Name the injustice that makes you doubt God most. Write it down, and write beside it: “The sentence is not forgotten.”
body: Pitgam is an official sentence — a decree from a throne. In the tagged Hebrew text it appears only here: the sentence against evil “is not executed speedily.” Men read the delay as absence and grow bold. But a decree not yet carried out is still a decree. For the man in Christ, the sentence against his sin was not delayed; it was executed at the cross, on the One who stood in his place. That is why the wait for justice does not have to terrify you.

stations.verse: Then I commended mirth, because a man has no better thing under the sun, than to eat, and to drink, and to be joyful: for that will accompany him in his labor all the days of his life which God has given him under the sun.
stations.question: Where are you so anxious about tomorrow that you are missing the good God has given you today?
stations.gloss: to praise, to laud, to commend
stations.live: At one meal each day this week, name the food in front of you and thank God for it out loud before you eat.
body: Shavach is to praise or commend. “Then I commended mirth.” The same verb turns up in the psalms as worship: “my lips shall praise you” (Psalm 63:3); “Extol him, all you peoples!” (Psalm 117:1). Solomon commends the simple joy of bread and drink because the future is not his to carry. When you stop carrying tomorrow, your mouth is free for praise. Worry and worship compete for the same breath.

stations.verse: Therefore don’t be anxious for tomorrow, for tomorrow will be anxious for itself. Each day’s own evil is sufficient.
stations.question: What tomorrow are you trying to live in right now?

stations.verse: then I saw all the work of God, that man can’t find out the work that is done under the sun, because however much a man labors to seek it out, yet he won’t find it. Yes even though a wise man thinks he can comprehend it, he won’t be able to find it.
stations.question: What work of God in your life are you refusing to trust until He explains it?
stations.live: Name one work of God in your life you cannot understand right now, and pray: “Your work is too deep for me, and You are good.”
body: Ma‘aseh is a work — something made or done. Solomon says the ma‘aseh of God cannot be found out; however hard the wise search, they cannot trace it. He said the same in 3:11: man “can’t find out the work that God has done.” This is not because God’s work is chaotic but because it is vast — “How great are your works, Yahweh! Your thoughts are very deep” (Psalm 92:5). The dust wants to audit God before it trusts. Faith bows before a work too deep to fathom and rests in the One doing it.

stations.verse: ‘For my thoughts are not your thoughts, and your ways are not my ways,’ says Yahweh. ‘For as the heavens are higher than the earth, so are my ways higher than your ways, and my thoughts than your thoughts.
stations.question: Where do you need to stop demanding that God’s work make sense before you trust it?
stations.live: Tell God one road you have insisted on this year. Pray Isaiah 55:7–9 over it, and ask for His way instead.
body: Derekh is a road — the path you walk and so the way you live. “Your ways are not my ways.” God’s roads run higher than yours, the way the heavens are higher than the earth. Solomon uses the word in 11:5: you do not know “the way of the wind,” and so you do not know the work of God. The verse just before Isaiah 55:8 invites the wicked to forsake his way and return to Yahweh, who “will freely pardon.” The higher way is a way of mercy.

stations.verse: We know that all things work together for good for those who love God, for those who are called according to his purpose.
stations.question: Which hidden work of God in your life do you most need to trust is for good?
pulls: You will not discover the pattern. But you can trust the One weaving it — the same God who worked His deepest purpose through a cross that looked like defeat.

practices.title: STOP AUDITING THE WORK OF GOD
practices.body: This week, notice where you are refusing to trust God until He explains Himself — demanding to understand the why before you will rest. Name it, and lay it down: “Father, Your work is too deep for me to trace, and I do not need to. I trust the Worker.”

practices.title: HOLD ON TO “IT WILL BE BETTER”
practices.body: When you see the wicked prosper or the righteous suffer this week, resist the conclusion that justice will never come. Anchor yourself in what Solomon knew even without the timeline: it will be better with those who fear God. Bring the injustice to God and leave the verdict — and the timing — in His hands.

practices.title: RECEIVE TODAY FROM THE SON
practices.body: You cannot live in tomorrow, so stop trying. When anxiety pulls you into a future you cannot enter, come back to Jesus and to today: “Lord, You have given me this day, not tomorrow. I receive it, and I trust You with the rest.” Then look for the good God has placed in the day in front of you, and enjoy it.

practices.title: ASK THE SPIRIT TO SHIFT YOUR WEIGHT
practices.body: Trust is not gritting your teeth about the unknown — it is leaning your full weight on God, and the Spirit enables it. Each morning this week, pray one honest sentence: “Holy Spirit, help me stop leaning on my own understanding and lean on the Father today.” Then notice where the anxious grip on the future loosens.

practices.title: NAME YOUR UNKNOWN OUT LOUD
practices.body: The dust carries its fears of the future in secret, where they grow. This week, tell one trusted brother the unknown that most frightens you — and let him remind you who holds it. Fear named in the light and handed to God loses its grip.

title: What the Dust Cannot Discover
subtitle: when you cannot see the future or fathom the ways of God
keyVerse: then I saw all the work of God, that man can’t find out the work that is done under the sun, because however much a man labors to seek it out, yet he won’t find it. Yes even though a wise man thinks he can comprehend it, he won’t be able to find it.

passage.text: Who is like the wise man? And who knows the interpretation of a thing? A man’s wisdom makes his face shine, and the hardness of his face is changed.
I say, “Keep the king’s command!” because of the oath to God.
Don’t be hasty to go out of his presence. Don’t persist in an evil thing, for he does whatever pleases him,
for the king’s word is supreme. Who can say to him, “What are you doing?”
Whoever keeps the commandment shall not come to harm, and his wise heart will know the time and procedure.
For there is a time and procedure for every purpose, although the misery of man is heavy on him.
For he doesn’t know that which will be; for who can tell him how it will be?

There is no man who has power over the spirit to contain the spirit; neither does he have power over the day of death. There is no discharge in war; neither shall wickedness deliver those who practice it.
All this I have seen, and applied my mind to every work that is done under the sun. There is a time in which one man has power over another to his hurt.
So I saw the wicked buried. Indeed they came also from holiness. They went and were forgotten in the city where they did this. This also is vanity.
Because sentence against an evil work is not executed speedily, therefore the heart of the sons of men is fully set in them to do evil.
Though a sinner commits crimes a hundred times, and lives long, yet surely I know that it will be better with those who fear God, who are reverent before him.
But it shall not be well with the wicked, neither shall he lengthen days like a shadow, because he doesn’t fear God.

There is a vanity which is done on the earth, that there are righteous men to whom it happens according to the work of the wicked. Again, there are wicked men to whom it happens according to the work of the righteous. I said that this also is vanity.

Then I commended mirth, because a man has no better thing under the sun, than to eat, and to drink, and to be joyful: for that will accompany him in his labor all the days of his life which God has given him under the sun.
When I applied my heart to know wisdom, and to see the business that is done on the earth (even though eyes see no sleep day or night),

then I saw all the work of God, that man can’t find out the work that is done under the sun, because however much a man labors to seek it out, yet he won’t find it. Yes even though a wise man thinks he can comprehend it, he won’t be able to find it.

stationsLabel: THE WORD ON THE HIDDEN WAYS OF GOD
stationsIntro: Read each passage slowly, with your Bible open if you can. Do not rush to the question. Let the verse land first, then answer honestly in the lines provided — and where a Hebrew word is opened up, let it sharpen the verse you just read.
lifeTitle: Where the Hidden Ways of God Meet Real Life
lifeIntro: This week is not about resigning yourself to a random universe — it is about resting in a God whose work is too deep to fathom and too good to doubt. It means leaning your whole weight on the One who holds the future you cannot see.
prayer: Father, I cannot see or control tomorrow. I hand it to You, who hold it. Your ways are higher than mine. Lord Jesus, You bore the sentence against my sin. You give me grace for today, and I will not live in a future You have not given. Holy Spirit, help me lean my whole weight on God and trust the work I cannot trace. Amen.
prayerLines: Father, I cannot see or control tomorrow.
I hand it to You, who hold it.
Your ways are higher than mine.
Lord Jesus, You bore the sentence against my sin.
You give me grace for today,
and I will not live in a future You have not given.
Holy Spirit, help me lean my whole weight on God
and trust the work I cannot trace. Amen.
bottomLine: The future and the day of your death are in God’s hands, and the wisest mind cannot pry them loose. What you cannot discover, He knows; what you cannot control, He holds. Move your weight off your own understanding and onto the God who proved His heart at a cross.
benediction: Before this week asks you to trust, it wants you to admit what you cannot do. The wisest man who ever lived, straining every nerve of his mind, confessed that the work of God cannot be found out — that the future is closed to him, the day of death beyond his power, the ways of God deeper than he can trace. That confession sounds at first like defeat. But it is the doorway to rest. The dust wears itself out trying to discover what God never meant it to carry.

So lift up your eyes. When you cannot see what tomorrow holds, lift up your eyes — the future you cannot discover is fully known to the God who holds it. When justice seems delayed and the wicked seem to win, lift up your eyes — it will be better with those who fear God, for the sentence is not forgotten. When the work of God in your life makes no sense, lift up your eyes — His ways are higher than yours, and His higher way is the way of mercy.

This is dust to revival, and it turns here: a soul that has stopped demanding to understand. You were never meant to trace God’s work, only to trust His heart — and He showed you His heart when His Son was lifted up on a cross. Lean your whole weight on Him.
closingVerse: You cannot find out the work of God, and you do not have to. You can trust the One who showed you His heart at a cross.
carry: Where are you refusing to rest until God explains Himself?

pulls: Because the grave is coming for everyone, today matters more, not less. Do the thing in front of you with all your might, and give your one life to what death cannot erase.
paras: Solomon has spent eight chapters emptying your hands. Now, near the end of his search, he says the most leveling thing of all: “All things come alike to all. There is one event to the righteous and to the wicked ... As is the good, so is the sinner” (9:2). Death does not check your résumé. The saint and the scoundrel arrive at the same ground. Under the sun, the great equalizer is the grave, and no amount of righteousness or wickedness changes the appointment.

This is not Solomon denying eternity — he is speaking of what the eye can see, life under the sun. And from that vantage, the sameness of death is a hard fact. “For the living know that they will die, but the dead don’t know anything” (9:5). You spend your days trying not to look at this, but Solomon presses your face toward it for a reason. If the grave is coming for everyone, then the question is not how to avoid it but what you will do with the breath you still have.

And here his answer turns, unexpectedly, toward life. “Whatever your hand finds to do, do it with your might; for there is no work, nor plan, nor knowledge, nor wisdom, in Sheol, where you are going” (9:10). Because the grave is real, today matters more, not less. Solomon is not preaching despair; he is preaching urgency. “Go your way — eat your bread with joy, and drink your wine with a merry heart; for God has already accepted your works” (9:7). The dust that has faced its own end is finally free to live. And for the man in Christ, the leveling grave has lost its sting, because Jesus died your death and rose to give you a life the grave cannot touch.

parts.label: PART ONE
parts.heading: THE GREAT LEVELER
paras: Solomon looks squarely at the one fact every culture works overtime to hide: everyone dies, and death does not sort you by merit. “There is one event to the righteous and to the wicked” (9:2), he says, echoing 2:14. From the standpoint of what happens under the sun, the funeral comes for the good and the evil alike. This is the dust at its most honest — refusing to pretend that being decent buys an exemption from the grave.

For the believer, this is not the whole story, but it is a necessary one. Death came into the world through Adam’s sin (Genesis 3; Romans 5). Even the Christian, who no longer fears death because Christ has drawn its sting, still must die. Solomon will not let you live in denial. He makes you look at the leveling grave — not to crush you, but to strip away every false hope so that you will build your life on the only foundation death cannot shake.

parts.label: PART TWO
parts.heading: DO IT WITH YOUR MIGHT
paras: Then comes the turn that makes this chapter surprisingly full of life. Having stared at death, Solomon does not counsel paralysis; he counsels wholehearted living. “Whatever your hand finds to do, do it with your might” (9:10). Do the work in front of you fully, now, because the time to do it is short and there is “no work” in Sheol. The reality of the grave is not a reason to give up. It is a reason to pour yourself into today.

This is the paradox at the heart of a well-lived life: the man most ready to die is the man most free to live. Because your days are numbered, they are precious; because the grave is real, the breath you have right now is a gift not to be squandered. Solomon is not preaching frantic distraction — he is preaching the freedom of a soul that has made peace with its mortality and now receives each day as the good gift it is.

parts.label: PART THREE
parts.heading: TIME AND CHANCE
paras: Solomon adds one more humbling truth: outcomes are not in your control. “The race is not to the swift, nor the battle to the strong ... but time and chance happen to them all” (9:11). The fastest runner does not always win; the strongest army does not always prevail; the wisest do not always prosper. You like to believe effort guarantees results, but Solomon has watched too long to believe it. “For man also doesn’t know his time” (9:12) — the net falls suddenly, and no one schedules the day it comes.

This could breed fatalism, but for the believer it breeds trust. What looks like time and chance from below is providence from above. What seems like random fortune is the ordered work of the God who holds your times (Psalm 31:15). So do your part with all your might — and release the outcome to Him, refusing both the pride that thinks it controls results and the despair that thinks no one does. “A man’s heart plans his course, but Yahweh directs his steps” (Proverbs 16:9).

parts.label: PART FOUR
parts.heading: WISDOM BETTER THAN STRENGTH
paras: Solomon closes with a small, unforgettable parable. A great king besieges a little city, and a poor wise man in it delivers the whole city by his wisdom — “yet no man remembered that same poor man” (9:15). The world runs on strength and shouting, and it forgets the quiet wisdom that actually delivers. “Wisdom is better than strength,” and “the words of the wise heard in quiet are better than the cry of him who rules among fools” (9:16–17).

The story carries a gospel shape, even though Solomon does not name it. A city was delivered by a poor, forgotten wise man — and the world would be saved by One of whom Isaiah said, “He has no good looks or majesty” (Isaiah 53:2), despised and rejected, whose quiet wisdom the shouting rulers could not hear. The dust chases strength and noise and fame; God saves through a poor Man on a cross. So do not measure your one life by the world’s loud scoreboard. Give it, quietly and wholly, to the King the world forgot.

stations.verse: All things come alike to all. There is one event to the righteous and to the wicked; to the good, to the clean, to the unclean, to him who sacrifices, and to him who doesn’t sacrifice. As is the good, so is the sinner; he who takes an oath, as he who fears an oath. This is an evil in all that is done under the sun, that there is one event to all: yes also, the heart of the sons of men is full of evil, and madness is in their heart while they live, and after that they go to the dead.
stations.question: Where are you living as if being good enough will exempt you from the grave?
stations.live: Read John 10:17–18 this week. Thank Christ that His death was chosen, and that it has changed what death means for you.
body: Miqreh is what befalls you — an event that happens to a man. The Preacher uses it for death: “one event happens to them all” (2:14), to the wise and the fool, to man and beast (3:19), to the righteous and the wicked (9:2). It is the word for what you cannot dodge. Under the sun, miqreh is the last word. But one death was not a miqreh at all. Jesus said no one took His life from Him; He laid it down, and He took it up again.

stations.verse: Go your way—eat your bread with joy, and drink your wine with a merry heart; for God has already accepted your works.
stations.question: What good thing has God given you today that you are too braced against the future to receive?
stations.gloss: to be pleased with, to accept with favor
stations.live: Before one meal each day this week, say, “I am accepted in Christ,” and then eat with a merry heart.
body: Ratsah is to accept with favor — to be pleased with someone. “God has already accepted your works.” Jacob used it when Esau received him: “you were pleased with me” (Genesis 33:10). David prayed it: “Be pleased, Yahweh, to deliver me” (Psalm 40:13). Solomon says eat your bread with joy because God has already accepted. In Christ that word lands fully: you are accepted before you work, so your work can be joy instead of a bid for favor.

stations.verse: Whatever your hand finds to do, do it with your might; for there is no work, nor plan, nor knowledge, nor wisdom, in Sheol, where you are going.
stations.question: What is the one thing in front of you this week that you could pour yourself into wholly?
stations.gloss: Sheol, the grave, the realm of the dead
stations.live: Let the reality of the grave sharpen today: do one good thing this week that you have been putting off, and do it with your might.
body: Sheol is the Old Testament name for the place of the dead — where, Solomon says, there is “no work, nor plan, nor knowledge, nor wisdom.” Jacob expected to go down to Sheol mourning his son (Genesis 37:35). But the same word carries the Bible’s deepest hope: “you will not leave my soul in Sheol” (Psalm 16:10). Peter quoted that verse at Pentecost and said it was spoken of the risen Christ (Acts 2:27). Jesus went down to death and came back out. For those who are His, the grave is no longer a wall.

stations.verse: I returned and saw under the sun that the race is not to the swift, nor the battle to the strong, neither yet bread to the wise, nor yet riches to men of understanding, nor yet favor to men of skill; but time and chance happen to them all.
stations.question: Where are you trusting your own speed, strength, or skill to guarantee an outcome?
stations.live: Name the outcome you are gripping hardest this week. Do your part fully, then pray: “The result is Yours.”
body: Pega is a chance occurrence — something that just happens to you. “Time and chance happen to them all.” In the tagged Hebrew text it appears only here. It names what the swift and the strong cannot plan around. From under the sun, pega is luck. From the throne, nothing is luck. The same God who numbered your hairs holds every pega in His hand. You do your part with all your might, and you leave the outcome to Him.

stations.verse: Then I said, ‘Wisdom is better than strength.’ Nevertheless the poor man’s wisdom is despised, and his words are not heard. The words of the wise heard in quiet are better than the cry of him who rules among fools.
stations.question: Where are you chasing the loud scoreboard instead of the quiet wisdom that actually delivers?
stations.live: Spend fifteen minutes in quiet before God one morning this week, no phone, no noise. Read Isaiah 30:15 and ask Him to make you a quiet man.
body: Nachat is quietness — rest, a settled calm. “The words of the wise heard in quiet” outweigh the shouting ruler. Solomon used it in 4:6 too: better a handful with quietness. Isaiah 30:15 puts it at the center of salvation: “You will be saved in returning and rest. Your strength will be in quietness and in confidence.” Then comes the sad line: “You refused.” Quiet trust looks weak to the world. God calls it strength.

stations.verse: ‘Death, where is your sting? Hades, where is your victory?’ The sting of death is sin, and the power of sin is the law. But thanks be to God, who gives us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ.
stations.question: How does the resurrection change the way you face your own death?

stations.verse: And whatever you do, work heartily, as for the Lord, and not for men,
stations.question: What task this week could you do heartily, as for the Lord and not for men?
pulls: The grave levels everyone, but Christ went down into it and came back out. Give your one life, quietly and wholly, to the King the world forgot.

practices.title: FACE THE GRAVE, THEN LIVE
practices.body: This week, let the reality of your own mortality make you more alive, not less. Ask honestly: “If my days are numbered, what am I wasting, and what deserves my whole heart?” Then give yourself fully to one good thing today — not frantically, but freely, as a man who has made peace with death in Christ.

practices.title: DO THE NEXT THING WITH YOUR MIGHT
practices.body: Stop waiting for the perfect conditions to give your best. This week, take the ordinary task in front of you — the work, the service, the duty — and pour yourself into it as for the Lord. Wholehearted faithfulness in today’s small thing is how a numbered life is well spent.

practices.title: RELEASE THE OUTCOME TO THE SON
practices.body: You are not in charge of results. This week, when you catch yourself gripping an outcome you cannot control, hand it to Jesus: “Lord, I will do my part with all my might, and I release the results to You.” Do the work; trust Him with what it yields.

practices.title: ASK THE SPIRIT TO QUIET THE SCOREBOARD
practices.body: The world shouts that only the swift, strong, and loud matter. Each morning this week, pray: “Holy Spirit, quiet the world’s scoreboard in me, and let me give my life to the quiet wisdom that delivers.” Then notice where you can choose faithful obscurity over applause that will be forgotten anyway.

practices.title: RECEIVE TODAY AS ACCEPTED
practices.body: Solomon says God has already accepted your works — today is a gift to receive, not a test to pass. This week, deliberately enjoy one good thing God has given, with a grateful heart. And tell one trusted brother how you are learning to spend your one life on what death cannot erase.

title: One Fate, One Life
subtitle: when the grave levels everyone and today is the only day you have
keyVerse: Whatever your hand finds to do, do it with your might; for there is no work, nor plan, nor knowledge, nor wisdom, in Sheol, where you are going.

passage.text: For all this I laid to my heart, even to explore all this: that the righteous, and the wise, and their works, are in the hand of God; whether it is love or hatred, man doesn’t know it; all is before them.

All things come alike to all. There is one event to the righteous and to the wicked; to the good, to the clean, to the unclean, to him who sacrifices, and to him who doesn’t sacrifice. As is the good, so is the sinner; he who takes an oath, as he who fears an oath.

This is an evil in all that is done under the sun, that there is one event to all: yes also, the heart of the sons of men is full of evil, and madness is in their heart while they live, and after that they go to the dead.
For to him who is joined with all the living there is hope; for a living dog is better than a dead lion.
For the living know that they will die, but the dead don’t know anything, neither do they have any more a reward; for their memory is forgotten.
Also their love, their hatred, and their envy has perished long ago; neither do they any longer have a portion forever in anything that is done under the sun.
Go your way—eat your bread with joy, and drink your wine with a merry heart; for God has already accepted your works.
Let your garments be always white, and don’t let your head lack oil.

Live joyfully with the wife whom you love all the days of your life of vanity, which he has given you under the sun, all your days of vanity, for that is your portion in life, and in your labor in which you labor under the sun.
Whatever your hand finds to do, do it with your might; for there is no work, nor plan, nor knowledge, nor wisdom, in Sheol, where you are going.

I returned and saw under the sun that the race is not to the swift, nor the battle to the strong, neither yet bread to the wise, nor yet riches to men of understanding, nor yet favor to men of skill; but time and chance happen to them all.

For man also doesn’t know his time. As the fish that are taken in an evil net, and as the birds that are caught in the snare, even so are the sons of men snared in an evil time, when it falls suddenly on them.
I have also seen wisdom under the sun in this way, and it seemed great to me.
There was a little city, and few men within it; and a great king came against it, besieged it, and built great bulwarks against it.
Now a poor wise man was found in it, and he by his wisdom delivered the city; yet no man remembered that same poor man.
Then I said, “Wisdom is better than strength.” Nevertheless the poor man’s wisdom is despised, and his words are not heard.
The words of the wise heard in quiet are better than the cry of him who rules among fools.
Wisdom is better than weapons of war; but one sinner destroys much good.
Dead flies cause the oil of the perfumer to produce an evil odor; so does a little folly outweigh wisdom and honor.
A wise man’s heart is at his right hand, but a fool’s heart at his left.
Yes also when the fool walks by the way, his understanding fails him, and he says to everyone that he is a fool.
If the spirit of the ruler rises up against you, don’t leave your place; for gentleness lays great offenses to rest.
There is an evil which I have seen under the sun, the sort of error which proceeds from the ruler.
Folly is set in great dignity, and the rich sit in a low place.
I have seen servants on horses, and princes walking like servants on the earth.
He who digs a pit may fall into it; and whoever breaks through a wall may be bitten by a snake.
Whoever carves out stones may be injured by them. Whoever splits wood may be endangered by it.
If the ax is blunt, and one doesn’t sharpen the edge, then he must use more strength; but skill brings success.
If the snake bites before it is charmed, then is there no profit for the charmer’s tongue.
The words of a wise man’s mouth are gracious; but a fool is swallowed by his own lips.
The beginning of the words of his mouth is foolishness; and the end of his talk is mischievous madness.
A fool also multiplies words. Man doesn’t know what will be; and that which will be after him, who can tell him?
The labor of fools wearies every one of them; for he doesn’t know how to go to the city.
Woe to you, land, when your king is a child, and your princes eat in the morning!
Happy are you, land, when your king is the son of nobles, and your princes eat in due season, for strength, and not for drunkenness!
By slothfulness the roof sinks in; and through idleness of the hands the house leaks.
A feast is made for laughter, and wine makes the life glad; and money is the answer for all things.
Don’t curse the king, no, not in your thoughts; and don’t curse the rich in your bedroom: for a bird of the sky may carry your voice, and that which has wings may tell the matter.

stationsLabel: THE WORD ON ONE LIFE UNDER THE SUN
stationsIntro: Read each passage slowly, with your Bible open if you can. Do not rush to the question. Let the verse land first, then answer honestly in the lines provided — and where a Hebrew word is opened up, let it sharpen the verse you just read.
lifeTitle: Where the One Life Meets Real Life
lifeIntro: This week is not about morbid fear of the grave — it is about the freedom of a soul that has faced its mortality in Christ and is now free to live. It means doing today’s work with your might and releasing the outcome to God.
prayer: Father, my days are numbered, and my times are in Your hand. I receive today from You. Lord Jesus, You laid down Your life and took it up again. You took the sting out of death. I give my one life wholly to You. Holy Spirit, help me do today’s work with my might and leave the rest to God. Amen.
prayerLines: Father, my days are numbered,
and my times are in Your hand.
I receive today from You.
Lord Jesus, You laid down Your life and took it up again.
You took the sting out of death.
I give my one life wholly to You.
Holy Spirit, help me do today’s work with my might and leave the rest to God. Amen.
bottomLine: The grave levels everyone, and outcomes are not in your control. That is not a reason for despair; it is a reason to live. Do today’s work with your might, release the results to God, and rest in the risen Christ who took the sting out of death.
benediction: Before this week frees you to live, it makes you look at the one thing you most avoid. Solomon says it plainly: one event happens to all — the grave does not check your résumé, and the good and the evil arrive at the same ground. It is the great leveler, and the dust exhausts itself pretending it is not coming. But Solomon does not press your face toward the grave to crush you. He does it to set you free from every false hope, and free to live the one life you actually have.

So lift up your eyes. When the sameness of death tempts you to despair, lift up your eyes — God has accepted your works, so eat your bread with joy and do your work with your might. When you cannot control the outcome, lift up your eyes — your times are in His hand, and what looks like chance to you is providence to Him. When the world’s loud scoreboard shames your quiet faithfulness, lift up your eyes — the city was delivered by a forgotten wise man, and the world by a despised and risen One.

This is dust to revival, and it turns here: a soul that has faced the grave and been set free by the One who conquered it. “Death, where is your sting? Hades, where is your victory?” Christ went into the grave and came back out, and nothing you do in Him will be lost.
closingVerse: The grave levels everyone, but Christ turned it from a wall into a door.
carry: Where are you either denying the grave or paralyzed by it?

pulls: Every dead end in this book was clearing the ground for one command: remember your Creator. The whole restless search was always a road home to God.
paras: After twelve chapters of emptying your hands, Solomon finally opens his own — and points home. “Remember also your Creator in the days of your youth” (12:1). This is the word the whole book has been aching toward. Every dead end — pleasure, wisdom, work, wealth, the grave — was clearing the ground for this one command. Not a better strategy under the sun, but remembering the One above it. The dust was made by a Creator, and it will never rest until it turns back to Him.

Then Solomon writes one of the most sobering poems in Scripture: a picture of aging and death. The light is darkened, the keepers of the house tremble, the grinders cease because they are few, the daughters of music are brought low (12:2–4). He is describing, tenderly and unflinchingly, the slow closing of a life — failing eyes, bending back, fading strength — until “the silver cord is severed ... and the dust returns to the earth as it was, and the spirit returns to God who gave it” (12:6–7). You came from dust; to dust you return. Remember your Creator now, while you still have strength to serve Him, before the evil days come.

And then, in a single sentence, Solomon gathers up everything and lands it: “This is the end of the matter. All has been heard. Fear God and keep his commandments; for this is the whole duty of man” (12:13). After all the vapor, all the striving, all the ache — this. The entire book has been a long argument that nothing under the sun can satisfy a soul made for the God above it, and this is the conclusion the argument was built to reach. “For God will bring every work into judgment” (12:14). Your one life is not vapor after all, because it is lived before a God who sees, and everything counts.

parts.label: PART ONE
parts.heading: REMEMBER HIM NOW
paras: “Remember also your Creator in the days of your youth.” The urgency is in the timing: now, while you have strength, clarity, and years. Solomon is not telling the young to enjoy sin while they can — he has spent twelve chapters demolishing that lie. He is telling every soul with breath in it to turn to God today, before the strength to serve Him fades. Do not wait for the years of which you will say, “I have no pleasure in them.” Remember your Maker while you still can.

This is a mercy aimed straight at procrastination — the quiet assumption that you will get serious about God later, after you have chased a few more things under the sun. Solomon, at the end of a long life of chasing, says: do not. In Scripture, remembering is more than recalling. When “God remembered Noah” (Genesis 8:1), He made the waters go down. To remember your Creator is to turn your life toward Him and live as His creature, now, today, before the light dims.

parts.label: PART TWO
parts.heading: DUST RETURNS TO DUST
paras: Solomon’s poem of aging ends where Genesis said it would: “the dust returns to the earth as it was, and the spirit returns to God who gave it” (12:7). “You are dust, and you shall return to dust” (Genesis 3:19). This is the verse the whole Soul Dust series has been circling. You are dust — formed from the ground, bound for the ground. The psalmist prayed, “My soul clings to the dust” (Psalm 119:25, NKJV), and this is why: dust is exactly what you are.

But look closely at the two halves of that verse. The dust returns to the earth — that is death, the wages of sin. The spirit returns “to God who gave it” — you are not only dust. And through Christ the second half answers the first. The same prayer goes on, “Revive me according to Your word,” and it is answered by the One who took on human dust, died, and rose. The dust that remembers its Creator does not fear its return to the ground, because it knows whose hands it is returning to.

parts.label: PART THREE
parts.heading: THE END OF THE MATTER
paras: Now Solomon steps back and delivers the verdict the whole book was written to reach: “Fear God and keep his commandments; for this is the whole duty of man” (12:13). Everything — the vapor, the ache, the dead ends, the search — comes down to this. Not a technique for a satisfied life under the sun, but reverent, obedient life before the God above it. Fear God. That is the whole of it.

You met the fear of God back in week two as the beginning of wisdom; here it is the end — the sum, the conclusion, the whole duty. The book that began “Vanity of vanities” ends “Fear God,” and that is the whole book in two phrases: everything under the sun is vapor, so turn and revere the God above it. This is not grim resignation. It is the deepest rest a dusty soul can find — to stop chasing and start worshiping, a creature gladly bent before his Creator.

parts.label: PART FOUR
parts.heading: EVERY WORK BEFORE GOD
paras: Solomon’s final word turns the whole book on its head: “For God will bring every work into judgment, with every hidden thing, whether it is good, or whether it is evil” (12:14). If everything is vapor, nothing you do matters. But if God will judge every work — then nothing you do is vapor after all. Your one life is lived before the face of a God who sees, and every hidden thing counts.

And here the whole search finds its rest in Christ. If God judges every work, the dust is in trouble — for who could stand? But the gospel Ecclesiastes was aching toward is this: Jesus took the judgment your works deserved, so that the man who comes to God through the Son is not condemned but welcomed. He “doesn’t come into judgment, but has passed out of death into life” (John 5:24). The Preacher’s last word is judgment — and the gospel’s answer is a cross where judgment fell on your Substitute. So you fear God not with the terror of the guilty but with the awe of the forgiven. The search is over. It ends where it always should have begun: in Him.

stations.verse: Remember also your Creator in the days of your youth, before the evil days come, and the years draw near, when you will say, ‘I have no pleasure in them;’
stations.question: Where have you been putting off turning your life toward God, assuming you will get serious later?
stations.gloss: to remember, to call to mind
stations.live: Pick one daily moment this week — waking, a meal, the drive — and turn your whole self toward your Creator there, out loud.
body: Zakar is to remember. In Scripture, God’s remembering is never idle: “God remembered Noah,” and the waters went down (Genesis 8:1). So to zakar your Creator is not to think of Him now and then but to turn your whole life toward Him. And the tender side is this: God zakars you too — “He remembers that we are dust” (Psalm 103:14). The dust that remembers its Creator is remembered by Him.

stations.verse: and the dust returns to the earth as it was, and the spirit returns to God who gave it.
stations.question: How does holding both halves of this verse together change the way you face your own death?

stations.verse: This is the end of the matter. All has been heard. Fear God and keep his commandments; for this is the whole duty of man.
stations.question: What is the one area of your life where “fear God and keep his commandments” most needs to become real this week?
stations.live: Write one sentence this week that finishes, “At the end of my life, I want it to be true that I…” Pray it back to God.
body: Soph is the end — the conclusion, where a thing comes out. “This is the end of the matter.” The Preacher used it twice before: man can’t find out God’s work “from the beginning even to the end” (3:11), and the house of mourning is “the end of all men” (7:2). Now he gives you the end you could not find: fear God. The end of your search is not a discovery. It is a Person to revere. And the end of your life, for the man in Christ, is not the grave but the Father’s house.

Mitsvah is a commandment — a word laid on you by one with the right to command. “Whoever keeps the commandment shall not come to harm” (8:5). Moses told Israel not to add to God’s word or take from it, but to “keep the commandments of Yahweh your God” (Deuteronomy 4:2). Solomon ends the book on it. For the man in Christ, keeping the commandments is not how you earn God. Christ kept them in your place. Now obedience is how a forgiven son walks home.
moreStudies.live: Name one clear command of God you have been ignoring. Obey it this week, and thank Christ for keeping it perfectly for you.

stations.verse: For God will bring every work into judgment, with every hidden thing, whether it is good, or whether it is evil.
stations.question: How does living before the face of God change what you do in secret?
stations.gloss: judgment, justice, the verdict of a judge
stations.live: Bring one hidden thing into the light this week — confess it to God, and if needed to a trusted brother. Then rest in the verdict Christ bore.
body: Mishpat is judgment — the verdict and the justice behind it. Solomon saw wickedness “in the place of justice” (3:16) and ends by promising that God will bring every work into mishpat. Abraham asked the question every man asks: “Shouldn’t the Judge of all the earth do right?” (Genesis 18:25). The answer is yes. And that is why the cross is good news: God did right, and the judgment for your sin fell on Christ.

stations.verse: ‘Come to me, all you who labor and are heavily burdened, and I will give you rest. Take my yoke upon you, and learn from me, for I am gentle and humble in heart; and you will find rest for your souls. For my yoke is easy, and my burden is light.’
stations.question: Where do you most need to stop laboring under the sun and come to Christ for rest this week?

stations.verse: ‘Most certainly I tell you, he who hears my word and believes him who sent me has eternal life, and doesn’t come into judgment, but has passed out of death into life.
stations.question: How does passing out of death into life turn your fear of judgment into the awe of the forgiven?
stations.gloss: to pass over, to move from one place to another
stations.live: Read John 5:24 aloud each morning this week. Thank Christ that you have already passed out of death into life.
body: Metabainō is to pass over — to move from one place to another. The city begged Jesus to “depart from their borders” (Matthew 8:34). John uses it for the hour when Jesus would “depart from this world to the Father” (John 13:1). And in 5:24 it is what happens to you when you believe: you have “passed out of death into life.” Solomon ended at the grave. Christ carries the believer across it, and the crossing is already done.
pulls: The book that began “Vanity of vanities” ends “Fear God.” The whole restless search comes home here, to your Creator, through Christ.

practices.title: REMEMBER YOUR CREATOR TODAY
practices.body: Stop waiting for later to get serious about God. This week, turn your whole life toward your Creator now — pick one daily moment and use it to live as His creature on purpose. Remembering God is not a feeling to summon but a direction to face. Face Him today, while you have breath and strength to serve Him.

practices.title: MAKE THE FEAR OF GOD THE BOTTOM LINE
practices.body: Everything in Ecclesiastes comes down to “fear God and keep his commandments.” This week, let that be the sum of your walk — not a grim duty but a glad reverence. Take the one area where you have been living as your own god, and bend the knee: “You are God, and I am not. I fear You and I will follow.”

practices.title: COME TO THE SON FOR REST
practices.body: The whole book has been a search for rest the world could not give — and Christ offers it freely. This week, take the heaviest burden you have carried through these twelve weeks and bring it to Jesus: “I have labored under the sun long enough. I come to You for rest.” Then actually lay it down.

practices.title: ASK THE SPIRIT TO MAKE YOU LIVE BEFORE GOD’S FACE
practices.body: God sees every work, even the hidden ones — and that truth, in the Spirit, becomes freedom, not fear. Each morning this final week, pray: “Holy Spirit, help me live today before the face of God — as a forgiven son, doing even small and hidden things for Him.” Then watch how the smallest deed gains weight.

practices.title: PRAY THE ANCHOR VERSE WITH A BROTHER
practices.body: You have named the dust for twelve weeks. Now close the way the study began. Pray it aloud — “My soul clings to the dust; Revive me according to Your word” (Psalm 119:25, NKJV) — and let the risen Christ be your revival. Then tell one trusted brother what God has done in you through this study.

title: Remember Your Creator
subtitle: when the whole search finally comes home to God
keyVerse: This is the end of the matter. All has been heard. Fear God and keep his commandments; for this is the whole duty of man.

passage.text: Cast your bread on the waters; for you shall find it after many days.
Give a portion to seven, yes, even to eight; for you don’t know what evil will be on the earth.
If the clouds are full of rain, they empty themselves on the earth; and if a tree falls toward the south, or toward the north, in the place where the tree falls, there shall it be.
He who observes the wind won’t sow; and he who regards the clouds won’t reap.
As you don’t know what is the way of the wind, nor how the bones grow in the womb of her who is with child; even so you don’t know the work of God who does all.
In the morning sow your seed, and in the evening don’t withhold your hand; for you don’t know which will prosper, whether this or that, or whether they both will be equally good.
Truly the light is sweet, and it is a pleasant thing for the eyes to see the sun.
Yes, if a man lives many years, let him rejoice in them all; but let him remember the days of darkness, for they shall be many. All that comes is vanity.

Rejoice, young man, in your youth, and let your heart cheer you in the days of your youth, and walk in the ways of your heart, and in the sight of your eyes; but know that for all these things God will bring you into judgment.
Therefore remove sorrow from your heart, and put away evil from your flesh; for youth and the dawn of life are vanity.
Remember also your Creator in the days of your youth, before the evil days come, and the years draw near, when you will say, “I have no pleasure in them;”
Before the sun, the light, the moon, and the stars are darkened, and the clouds return after the rain;
in the day when the keepers of the house shall tremble, and the strong men shall bow themselves, and the grinders cease because they are few, and those who look out of the windows are darkened,
and the doors shall be shut in the street; when the sound of the grinding is low, and one shall rise up at the voice of a bird, and all the daughters of music shall be brought low;

yes, they shall be afraid of heights, and terrors will be on the way; and the almond tree shall blossom, and the grasshopper shall be a burden, and desire shall fail; because man goes to his everlasting home, and the mourners go about the streets:
before the silver cord is severed, or the golden bowl is broken, or the pitcher is broken at the spring, or the wheel broken at the cistern,
and the dust returns to the earth as it was, and the spirit returns to God who gave it.
“Vanity of vanities,” says the Preacher. “All is vanity!”
Further, because the Preacher was wise, he still taught the people knowledge. Yes, he pondered, sought out, and set in order many proverbs.
The Preacher sought to find out acceptable words, and that which was written blamelessly, words of truth.
The words of the wise are like goads; and like nails well fastened are words from the masters of assemblies, which are given from one shepherd.
Furthermore, my son, be admonished: of making many books there is no end; and much study is a weariness of the flesh.
This is the end of the matter. All has been heard. Fear God and keep his commandments; for this is the whole duty of man.
For God will bring every work into judgment, with every hidden thing, whether it is good, or whether it is evil.

lifeTitle: Where the End of the Matter Meets Real Life
lifeIntro: This is the last week — and it is the one the whole study was written to reach. It is not about a new technique for living under the sun; it is about coming home to the God above it. Fear God, remember your Creator, and rest in Christ.
prayer: Father, I am dust, and I remember You, my Creator. I have chased the vapor long enough. I turn my whole life toward You. Lord Jesus, You bore my judgment. Because of You I have passed out of death into life. I come home to You for rest. Holy Spirit, help me fear God gladly and live this day before His face. Amen.

I have chased the vapor long enough.

bottomLine: The book that began “Vanity of vanities” ends “Fear God and keep his commandments.” Everything under the sun is vapor, so turn and revere the God above it. In Christ your return to God is not an end but a homecoming.
benediction: Twelve weeks ago you sat down in the dust and admitted the truth the Preacher named in his first breath: everything under the sun is vapor. You have watched the wisest man who ever lived chase pleasure, wisdom, work, wealth, and legacy — and come up empty in every one. You have faced the crooked places you cannot straighten, the future you cannot see, the grave that levels everyone. You have named the dust honestly, week after week. And now, at the end of the matter, Solomon points you home: remember your Creator. Fear God. This is the whole of it.

So lift up your eyes — one last time, and then for the rest of your life. When the vapor of the world tempts you back into the old chase, lift up your eyes — you were made for the God above the sun. When you feel the dust returning to dust, lift up your eyes — your spirit returns to the God who gave it, and in Christ the grave is a door. When you fear the judgment of every work, lift up your eyes — the judgment already fell on your Substitute, and the God you fear is the Father who welcomes you home.

This is dust to revival, and it ends where it was always going: a soul that clung to the ground, raised by the Christ who went into the ground for him and came out again. He has passed you out of death into life. The search is over. It ends in Him.
closingVerse: You clung to the dust and named it honestly for twelve weeks. The risen Christ is the revival the whole prayer was reaching for.
carry: What is the one thing God is calling you to do this week to remember your Creator?
